MR. FRASER-REJECTION OF QUESTIONS SUBMITTED FOR ORDER PAPER-STATEMENT OF MR. SPEAKER
speechtext:
The question of privilege raised yesterday by the hon. member for Peterborough West (Mr. Fraser) is very important as it bears upon one of the main privileges of members of parliament, namely the right to seek information on matters of administration for which the government is responsible to the House of Commons.

The hon. member sent in for the order paper a series of questions inquiring as to the number of motorcycles declared surplus by the army and air departments and asking how many of these vehicles had been disposed of through War Assets Corporation. The officer of the house whose duty it is to see that such questions are in order pointed out to the hon. member that the information sought could be obtained from the special committee on war expenditures and economies which was appointed on March 22 by the following resolution:
That a select committee be appointed to- examine the expenditure defrayed out of moneys provided by parliament for national defence and demobilization, and for other services directly connected with the war, including the disposal of surplus war assets, and to report what, if any, economies consistent with the execution of the policy decided by the government may be effected therein . . .
It seems, therefore, that the committee is the proper authority from which the information should be sought in connection with expenditures for defence, demobilization, and -please note-"for other services directly connected with the war, including the disposal of surplus war assets." The hon. member's questions come within the purview of the committee's powers. It is a well known principle in parliamentary procedure that the house cannot deal with matters referred to committees until those committtees have completed their work and reported to the house. I see in "May's Parliamentary Practice," 14th edition, recently published, the following as a type of question enumerated as being out of order:
Dealing with matters referred to a royal commission or with matters before a parliamentary committee or with matters within the juris-[DOT]diction of the chairman of a select committee or the authorities of the house. No question can be asked regarding proceedings in a committee which have not been placed before the house by a report from the committee.
Moreover the chairman of this committee on war expenditures and economies, the senior member for Halifax (Mr. Isnor) has invited all the members of the house to ask questions dealing with matters referred to the committee. On March 26, as reported in the minutes of the proceedings of that committee, he said that the hon. member for Eglinton (Mr. Fleming) had asked to appear before the committee and follow up a question placed on the order paper; and he added:
You are all familiar as to the answer given by the Minister of Reconstruction (Mr. Howe) yesterday, that Mr. Fleming would have the opportunity of asking the question before this committee. I have given this matter some thought, and I am just offering this to you as a suggestion, not* as a ruling. I am going to

Privilege-Mr. Fraser
suggest to you that you give Mr. Fleming an opportunity at once to place his questions on file here with a view to having them answered, but in the future I ain going to suggest that other members of parliament who are not members of this committee should pass along their questions either to the chairman or to another member whom they may select to place them before the committee. I think that in fairness to the members of this particular committee, Mr. Fleming arid others should follow that suggestion so as to give our own members an equal opportunity to have questions answered which they have in mind and have had in mind for some time. There are some questions that Mr. Probe. Mr. Stewart and Mr. Shaw had before the committee last year that have not as yet been dealt with. I feel in fairness to them that my suggestion should be followed. Is it your pleasure that we hear Mr. Fleming to-day with that understanding as to future members?"
The motion was carried; the hon. member for Eglinton thanked the chairman and submitted a series of questions. This was good parliamentary practice. A matter cannot be before a committee and before the house at the same time; and the proceedings of a committee should not be interfered with by answers to questions and reports laid on the table of the house.
In disallowing for the time being the hon. member's questions, I fully realize that his right to seek information is unimpeachable, but I am merely pointing out to him that he is following the wrong procedure. It is his privilege to file his questions with the chairman of the war expenditures and economies committee. I would therefore ask the hon. member for Peterborough West to try the committee, and if he does not succeed there, he will be free to adopt any course which will be open to him under the rules of the house.

Mr. Speaker, I wish only to make a constructive suggestion. In our opinion this is a very important matter, one which goes to the very root of the rights of hon. members of the House of Commons, namely that of asking a question at the proper stage. I point out to Your Honour, with great deference, that in applying common sense to the rule affecting questions asked in the house respecting proceedings before a committee I believe Your Honour should not go so far as to rule out any questions asked in the House of Commons just because a committee might have jurisdiction to deal with a wide variety of subjects. There is a vast difference between the proceedings currently before a committee, and the jurisdiction such committee may exercise, which may never reach the points, of questions the hon. member for Peterborough West or other hon. members may ask here.
The other point is this, if I may say so, that if that ruling were adhered to-and I am hopeful that Your Honour, with your usual fairness, will not hold us too closely to it-

It seems to me that this interferes with the rights of hon. members who are not serving on committees. If one is a member of a committee he can ask questions; 'but one cannot attend before all committees. If an hon. member has five questions to ask, he cannot be on five different committees at one time.

Mr. Speaker, I rise to a question of privilege with reference to the accuracy of the answers given to certain questions which I placed upon the order paper. On Thursday, July 11, an order of the House of Commons was tabled in answer to questions which had been standing in my name since May 27, 1946. Two of these questions were as follows:
1.	How many houses are being built on No. 2 highway near Port Hope under the Veterans Land Act?
2.	When will they be completed?
The answers tabled were as follows:
1.	Four.
2.	Houses are completed except for hardwood flooring, which is now being laid, and electrical connection with the hydro-electric power line.
My question of privilege is this: We in this house should be able to rely upon the accuracy of answers tabled in the house; yet a personal inspection of the houses in question made on Sunday, July 14, after the reply was tabled, showed that the houses are by no means complete, having nothing inside them except the studding and sub-floors. The following yet remains to be done:	Wallboard, with the
exception of one house, has not been completed; no plastering, painting, cupboards, doors, plumbing, trim and many other items necessary to make the structures complete. I would like an explanation of these inaccuracies and a proper reply to my question tabled.

Right Hon. L. S. ST. LAURENT (Minister of Justice): May I be permitted to answer a question submitted yesterday by the hon. member for Vancouver South (Mr. Green). The question was as follows:
I should like to direct a question to the Minister of Trade and Commerce. A Canadian Press dispatch published this morning indicates that a conference may be held this fall to consider the whole question of empire trade preferences. Will the minister make a statement in that regard?
The answer is as follows:	There have
been no arrangements made for a commonwealth conference on empire trade preferences this fall. speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I wish to make a brief statement on the Ontario winter wheat policy.
During the crop year 1945-46, Ontario winter wheat was sold at a ceiling price of $1,26. per bushel for No. 1 Canada eastern winter wheat, basis delivered at Montreal. There was an appropriate flour ceiling. Producers were also given the proceeds of an Ontario wheat equalization fund, arising from collection of an equalization fee on the exports of Ontario winter wheat flour. To place a floor under these prices, the Canadian wheat board was empowered to buy No. 1 Canada eastern winter wheat at $1.25 per bushel, basis delivered at Montreal. No purchases by the board were necessary, because commercial interests bought the wheat at the ceiling price.
It had originally been intended to raise the ceiling on Ontario wheat to $1.35 per bushel for the crop year beginning July 1, 1946, and to permit a corresponding increase in the 63260-225i
domestic price of winter wheat flour and the products thereof, but in view of recent developments in price control policy this step is not being taken. Instead producers will receive at time of delivery an additional nine cents per bushel which will be paid by the Canadian wheat board on behalf of the government.
In addition, the wheat board will pay to producers at time of delivery an amount of five cents per bushel in lieu of any payment from the equalization fund that will be operated as before with the government absorbing any profit or loss therein. By this payment at time of delivery, the difficulties and expense of making a subsequent small payment will be avoided. It is felt that this system will be more satisfactory to the producers.
The net effect will therefore be that producers of Ontario wheat will receive, in addition to the price paid by the purchaser under the existing price ceiling, an amount of 14 cents, nine cents of which represents the equivalent of an increased price and five cents of which represents a fixed and final payment out of the Ontario wheat flour equalization fund. The Canadian wheat board will continue to maintain a floor at $1.25.
I should perhaps add, for the sake of clarity, that no adjustment is being made in the price ceiling on Ontario wheat or products made therefrom.

subsubtopic: DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, my colleagues in this group have covered practically all our objections and the
particularly weak points in this budget, as far as we view these points in the light of our platform and in the light of the economic and social principles which we believe will lead to security and the happiness of the vast majority of the Canadian people.
I wish to deal particularly with the budget proposals as they affect the farmer, and particularly the farmer in the west. It seems to me that in most countries, in most civilized countries in any event, the farmer is always the forgotten man, at any rate if we consider the broad principles of economics as contained in the national budget. The only provision in this budget concerning the farmer as such is the resolution that the farmer shall be allowed to average his income over a period of three years. While I am thankful for this concession, it is but a small dose of relief. The constituency which I have the honour to represent is purely an agricultural area. In my business and profession as a lawyer I represent farmers exclusively, and during the long years of practising my profession I have acquired an intimate knowledge of the farmer's business and especially of his financial and economic difficulties.
I may say that there are a large number of farmers in my constituency who are paying income tax, and it is a matter of very vital importance to them, especially during the last two years. During the parliamentary recess last winter I had occasion to talk to my constituents, my farmer constituents, about income tax in general. I heard numerous complaints and suggestions about farmers' income tax, and I have compiled these into six points which I shall place before the house and upon which I shall elaborate. I may say that these points, although I endorse them fully, are not my own but are those of the farmers in my constituency, and I deem it my bounden duty as their representative to place them before this house and before the minister.
Here are the points:
1. The farmer does not mind paying his share of the national tax load by way of income tax, provided that it is fairly, justly and equally imposed.
2.	He thinks that, because of the whims of nature-his is a very hazardous business, giving him a bountiful crop one year and practically nothing another year-his income should be averaged over a period of at least five years.
3.	The form of income tax returns which is required to be completed needs the employment of a bookkeeper and should be simplified.
4.	The actual assessments are delayed too long.
The Budget-Mr. Jaenicke

5.	Additional exemption should be allowed to a farmer who has the help of his wife and of his children, without whose help he could not have the income on which he is taxed.
6.	Some of his old debts should be allowed as deductions.
The first point I mentioned was that the farmer does not object to bear his fair and equitable burden, provided that he is satisfied that everyone else carries his load. The fact is that the farmer is not satisfied that everyone bears his fair share. A farmer who makes his return every year, because he has been requested to do so, has a feeling that some of his neighbours escape the arduous duty of filling in that form and of paying the tax. Of course he does not know, and often his suspicion is unfounded and the neighbour whom he suspects of delinquency may think the same of him. But in our province of Saskatchewan I am sure the tax-paying farmer knows that some persons are not making returns and are not paying their taxes, because they boast that they are not doing so; and some of these persons are the Saskatchewan taxpayers association-not to be confused with the income tax payers association. So far as I can gather, the officers of this association, and especially the secretary, claim that under our constitution as it stands, or as it should stand, according to his contention, the dominion has no authority to collect income tax. I offer no opinion on this question, because, I mention later, the matter is sub judice, and being a lawyer I have the greatest respect for judicial decisions. So far as I am concerned the question has already been decided. It was decided in 1924 by the privy council. The fact remains, however, that many people, especially farmers, because of the feeling that the tax is not fairly and justly borne rather than because of the intricate constitutional question, have joined the association. This has gone on now for almost two years, so far as I can find out, and only within the last month has action been taken against the secretary. He advised me that he had been prosecuted last month and was defending the case on the constitutional ground. Yesterday I saw a clipping in the Saskatoon Star Phoenix reporting that his case came up last Friday and was adjourned again because apparently the attorney general for Canada had not yet acknowledged his notice that the constitutional question was to be raised, although he had received an acknowledgement from the attorney general of the province. This man is defending himself. I do not know whether he is without the means to retain a lawyer, or whether he is unable to get a lawyer to

review the matter and give an opinion. In any event, as I say, this man is defending his own case and his defence should be facilitated by the Department of National Revenue to bring the issue to an early conclusion.
I do not know this gentleman personally, and have never approached him by letter- that is the secretary of the association, Mr. Smith. But he saw the press dispatch in the Saskatoon Star Phoenix dealing with the answer I received from the ministry to a question I placed on the order paper three months ago, pertaining to the refusal of persons to file income tax returns on constitutional grounds. The question and answer will be found at page 421 of Hansard. I did not refer to the Saskatchewan Tax Payers Association in that question, by the way. However, he wrote to me, after seeing that press dispatch in the Saskatoon paper, and he states in part:
Just to keep the record straight, the Department of National Revenue have not to date proceeded against any member of our association. Numerous threats have been received. No action has been taken. We requested that the department produce its source of authority. They seemed reluctant to state.
Before I had time to reply to the letter, I had another from Mr. Smith dated April 8, 1946, in which he stated in part;
As the income tax division here in Saskatoon have been sending out multigraphed forms threatening to sue our members, it was necessary for us to get a form letter multigraphed to answer them. Enclosed is a copy.
The multigraphed letter form, of which the department must have received scores, perhaps hundreds, reads:
The inspector of income tax, Federal Building, Saskatoon, Sask. Attention Mr. W. S. Mackenzie.
Dear Sir:
Re Income Tax
I am a member of the Saskatchewan Tax Payers' Association which was organized last year to bring to the attention of the legislature the advantage and desirability of the province repossesing all rights to the collection of income tax. The dominion-provincial conference adjourned February 7 last without reaching a decision on this question. Prime Minister W. L. Mackenzie King in a letter to us states "that this matter has been referred to the Department of Justice for consideration and attention."	.	.
As the premiers are to meet again this month I am awaiting the results of this conference before making returns to your office.
I am, sir,
Yours truly,
I repeat, I offer no opinion on the constitutional question involved. I complain, however, that this matter has been allowed to drag along for almost two years, creating doubts in the minds of people, especially the farmers. In view of the publicity which the association

The Budget-Mr. Jaenicke
has received in the Saskatoon paper about it's contention, without action being taken to decide the issue, these doubts were reasonable doubts and I cannot blame any layman for joining the association if it offered some relief in respect of a tax which he feels is not justly and fairly borne by all the people. Likewise in one large area in my constituency the feeling of unfairness is particularly strong. It will surprise some members of the house to learn that there are several farmers in that portion of my constituency who were subject to excess profits tax, and they may still be in that category, although in last year's "budget some relief was granted them by the amendments to the excess profits tax legislation. These cases, I admit, are rare. However, here is an example. One farmer had an income a few years back of a little over $19,000. This is not excessive, because he farms over six sections with a cultivated area of over 4,000 acres. The minister took everything from him except $5,000. That is, on an income of a little over $19,000, he paid more than $14,000. He is one of the finest patriotic gentlemen I have ever had the pleasure of meeting. He did not complain because the tax was high, but he said in discussing his plight with me that he would not object if industry, especially monopolistic industry, bore a like burden, and he pointed to concessions by way of accelerated deductions in depreciation given to the Aluminum Company of Canada and other monopolies which are mostly foreign-owned corporations. He referred me to the capital gains made during the war by large industrial corporations after payment of taxes. No wonder the farmers are bitter about income tax.
I admit that this farmer is a fairly large operator, but being unable to replace worn-out machinery and to make depreciation deductions for machinery because it is too old, he is now faced with the necessity of acquiring new equipment as soon as it is available. But he was not allowed to set up a reserve in order to purchase the new equipment he now needs.
While this feature of the excess profits tax was eased somewhat, the feeling persists, and I believe rightly so, that the farmer, after many years of crop failure and disastrous economic conditions, is not fairly treated as compared with industry.
My second point is that the farmer should be entitled to average his income over a period of five years instead of three, as proposed by the minister. That period of three years may be sufficient to meet the needs of the farmer in the east, where the weather is not as capricious as it is on the prairies. Let me give one concrete example. A farmer in my constituency. who did not think he was liable for
income tax because according to his bank account he was going into the hole, was finally requested to make returns for 1942, 1943 and 1944. It took us a period of several months to get all the vouchers and accounts ready. The matter is now settled and this is the position. In 1942 he operated at a loss of $1,16058. He is a fairly large operator. In 1943, when most of his 1942 crop was marketed and when his 1943 crop was completely hailed out, his net income was $2,591.81, and in 1944 his net income was $1,180.29. He was not taxed. He is a married man. The inspector did allow the 1942 loss to be applied on the 1943 income, which left a small taxable income of $1,431.56 for 1943. As I have already said, the 1944 income was not taxable. The big headache comes in 1945. In that year he marketed almost $11,000 worth of cattle; and he was obliged to do so, not by choice but rather by force of circumstances. In . the fall of 1944, just when he had a bunch of cattle ready to take to market, a bottleneck developed in the packing plants and he was not able to sell his stock until early in 1945. Later that same year he had his regular allotment ready for market, and sold them. Then in the fall he found that because of crop failure in that particular district, resulting from drought, he had insufficient feed to carry all his cattle through the winter, and he was forced to sell a large number which he had intended to keep until 1946. So in one year he had to sell cattle which should have been sold over a period of three years. If you keep in mind his returns for the previous three years, it seems to me only just and reasonable that a farmer in this position should be allowed to average his income over a period of five years rather than three.
I venture to say that similar cases and similar circumstances can be duplicated a hundredfold. I can give the minister all the particulars and references in this case if he desires them. I dare say he has received numerous requests and resolutions from farmers and farm organizations asking for the five-year average. I sincerely believe the request is reasonable, and I trust the minister may give the matter further consideration and amend his resolution on that point accordingly.
My third point is the simplification of returns. I admit that the blue form on which a farmer computes his income is not complicated, and that with the records of his grain marketing permit book he can pretty well establish his gross income. The deductions, however, are a different matter. Very few farmers keep books; it just is not in them. It is not that they are incapable of doing so, but
The Budget-Mr. Jaenicke

they simply do not have time. Usually the farmer buys practically all his necessary supplies, his main supplies which cost a great deal of money, during his busiest season, when he is seeding, summer fallowing, harvesting, working from sunrise to sunset; when he has to rush to town for the necessary repairs in order to keep his outfit going, and at night he is too tired to make bookkeeping entries of the amounts he expended during the day. Over a period of days and weeks I have spent hours assisting farmers to complete their income tax returns. 1 have asked them to gather up their vouchers, accounts and so on; then, after spending two or three weeks on it and getting the form finally completed, a little later the farmer finds this cheque or that receipt, the particulars of which he forgot to give me at the time. Some suggestions have been made to me in this connection. The farmer says he wants a simplified form, and there is at least one suggestion that I think has some merit. I should like to submit it to the minister in the hope that it might be applied at Jeast to western grain farmers. Instead of itemizing his expenses, as he is now required to do, allow the farmer a flat reduction of a certain amount per cultivated acre, in which amount would be included all the necessary expenses and deductions which must now be itemized. I think with the assistance of organized agriculture and our agricultural colleges

that is, the departments of farm management of our colleges- the officers of the Department of National Revenue could arrive at some fair and equitable figure. It might have to be varied according to the size of the farm and the district or location, and according to the rise and fall of the cost of supplies the farmer has to buy, but I do not think any of these obstacles is insurmountable. I believe this suggestion is worth a trial on an optional basis at least, just as the "average" feature proposed by the minister is to be optional, if I understood his explanation aright.
The fourth point I have enumerated is the complaint that the assessments are too long delayed. I presume that is a general complaint and does not pertain only to farmers. I maintain, however, that it affects the farmer more than anyone else because of this lack of bookkeeping to which I referred a few moments ago. A person has a feeling of confidence when he has made his return and paid his tax, but this feeling is dissipated when three or four years later an assessment notice is received stating that large sums of money are still owing the Minister of Finance. In one case which has come to my notice, after some further assessments were made requiring the payment of several hundred dollars in

addition, considerable correspondence ensued and at one stage the inspector asked this man to submit a statement of assets and liabilities from 1938 to date. Surely that is an impossibility for a farmer who keeps no books, at least as far as the earlier years are concerned.
I would plead with the minister that if necessary a larger staff be employed in order that the assessments can be completed more quickly and the taxpayers may know exactly where they stand.
The fifth point concerns a matter that has been drawn to the minister's attention not only in this debate but in debates on numerous other subjects in this house; for instance, in the debate on the address in reply to the speech from the throne. It refers to exemptions for a farmer's wife, at least in cases where part of the income is derived from dairying and poultry, and also where the children of the farmer are helping, without remuneration, in the accumulation of the income that is taxed. I endorse whole-heartedly and fully the very able argument presented a few days ago by the hon. member for Selkirk (Mr. Bryce) in connection with this point. I think it is only fair, especially in view of the fact that agriculture is not yet receiving the share of our national income to which it is entitled.
The last point I enumerated concerned itself with the farmer's debts. In the first place I contend that he should be entitled to deduct in any year capital payments in respect of a mortgage or purchase agreement covering the half section of land on which he makes his home. I think it is pretty well agreed in western Canada that the smallest farm unit on which a farmer can make a decent living for himself and his family is 320 acres. I say that with the proviso that there should be parity prices, which the fafmer does not have to-day. In some districts in the west even a half section would not be enough land.
Secondly, in view of the difficulties the farmers experienced prior to 1938, I think they should be entitled to deduct the old [DOT]debts which they pay off. I believe it should be the policy of any government to assist farmers to get out of debt entirely. I know of no better class of consumers than the farmers, and a debt free agricultural class- and I mean just that, a debt free class- would be reflected in our whole economy by an increased home consumption of our industrial production, which has been emphasized by previous speakers in this debate. Let us do everything in our power to make agriculture debt free, though our present system of taxation is going a long way to prevent such a desirable end being achieved.

The Budget-Mr. Jaenicke
No doubt the minister and some hon. members will contend that my suggestions constitute a plea for special privileges for the farmers as a class. I do not admit the truth of this, but even if that argument should have some validity I think the suggestions made would work to the advantage of our whole economy; and I repeat that I know of no better way of distributing purchasing power than through the farmers. Furthermore I maintain that agriculture has been, is now and for some time to come will be the basic industry in our economy, and a prosperous agriculture will ensure prosperity for the whole of Canada. Then we must consider the uncertainties and hazards which agriculture has to face. There is the weather. In later years aviation has concerned itself a great deal about the weather, but the farmer has been battling and matching wits with the weather man ever since the dawn of history. There is hail, wind, frost and drought which are capable of destroying a whole year's hard labour. In the west we fight grasshoppers, gophers, sawflies, cutworms, rust, diseases of animals and diseases of plants. Nature seems to be full of these tricks, for no sooner have we built up a defence against these pests than some new ones come along. Then there is always uncertainty of the market and the future in general.
I think the farmer in his highly hazardous and speculative industry needs these considerations in relation to income tax liability. In addition he should have further protection of parity prices. I contend that these are not special privileges, but simply compensation for the extraordinary hazards of the farmer's highly important industry.
We had considerable discussion about parity prices at the last session, with everyone having a different idea as to what parity prices really meant. I confess the question has become confused. My rough idea on parity prices is that the farmer should receive his fair share of the national income. If the farming population of Canada comprises thirty per cent of the total population, agriculture should receive thirty per cent of the national income, or as near as possible to that percentage. I shall be frank to admit that this formula could only be a basis for computing parity prices for agriculture, but upon that basis I think the amount can be ascertained.
Of course the cost of production and the farmers' cost of living will have to be taken into consideration. In this connection I should like to mention tables contained in the Economic Annalist, which is a pamphlet received by all hon. members. It is sent to us by the
Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Gardiner), and upon it I wish to commend him highly. It is a splendid pamphlet, worthy of the study of every hon. member. In it is a table showing the rise and fall of agricultural prices as against the rise and fall of the cost of living and the cost of the goods and services the farmer has to buy. The suggestions which I have made are one little step in the right direction, if .they are adopted. subsubtopic: DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
(Translation): Mr. Speaker, I have a few remarks to make in connection with this debate. The Canadian ratepayer is greatly disappointed with the 1946-47 budget. He had expected that, in view of the considerable increase in the cost of living, especially from 1941 to 1946, the income tax exemption would be made applicable to incomes of 81,200 for single persons and $2,000 for man-ied people, effective from April 1st 1946. This has not been done. The government could have relieved the Canadian people much more than they are doing, by curtailing the expenditures
of some departments. I am amazed at the way the estimates are apportioned between the various departments.
We have a $2,769 million budget; of which $1,500 millions are for demobilization and re-eontruction, while 593 millions are earmarked for the Department of Finance. This amount of 593 millions includes 481 millions for interest on our public debt.
Mr. Speaker, I respectfully submit that reforms are needed in our financial system. The interest paid on the cost of public works, that is if projects carried out by our governments, whether federal, provincial, or municipal or by our school boards, is too high. I am agreeable that capital invested in useful private ventures invoking some risk should bring a reasonable return, but when it comes to the financial requirements of the government, our country's economic system should enable the latter to obtain the funds needed for just about the equivalent of the administrative costs.
Another department where an inquiry is particularly needed is the Department of National Defence. The minister (Mr. Abbott) requires for the administration of his department during 1946-47 a sum of $488,600,000, which sum is, of course, quite apart from the 525 millions requested by the Department of Veterans Affairs.
Expenditures of $488,200,000 for the army and for demobilization in this second peacetime year! To me this seems too much, especially when I scrutinize the various items. Here is the approximate break-down of those expenditures: Salaries, wages, pay and allowances, over 200 millions; transport of personnel and goods, 41 millions; furnishings, food and medical services, 37 million dollars; munitions, weapons, vehicles, 100 million dollars.
Mr. Speaker, I have brought these figures to the attention of the house and the public to show what becomes of our people's money and to prevent that essential social reforms be blamed1 for the heavy burden placed on the weary shoulders of the disappointed taxpayers.
As for cooperative associations, the sound representations which the various interested parties have made to me show how touchy this problem is, since we are asked to referee a struggle between interests that feel they are both opposite and1 legitimate. A basic factor must be our guide in these matters, and that is the general interest. The function of the state, Mr. Speaker, is to endeavour through legislation, to ensure the people they are called upon to administer, the greatest *possible degree of earthly happiness, and1 one of the essential elements of such happiness
The Budget-Mr. Ilamel

is the highest possible standard of living compatible with the economic possibilities of our country.
There are, without question, two ways of doing this: first, to raise the people's income; second, to bring down the cost of living. Now that is just what true cooperatives are striving to do. Through the elimination, as far as possible, of certain powerful middlemen who generally go in for speculation, the producer unquestionably gets better prices. For the consumer, on the other hand, and especially the industrial worker, increased buying power means that he is better able to obtain the necessities of life.
Mr. Speaker, cooperatives have prospered, especially among our people, because of the concern over the exodus of farmers to the cities. In 1937 and 1938, prominent sociologists made a survey of the exodus from the farms. They thus investigated 161 localities of the province of Quebec, and their findings are quite interesting even though alarming. Out of 161 localities they visited, the average family income was less than $600 in 126 municipalities. It was on the strength of those findings that our best sociologists urged the intensive development of our cooperatives.
What a sad and grave mistake it would be, Mr. Speaker, through arbitrary and meddlesome legislation, to interfere with the development of co-operatives which have been such a boon to our farmers and industrial workers. Besides, the various individuals who have submitted to us documents complaining of the cooperatives do not represent the mass of the people.
I have here a list of companies who sent briefs against the cooperatives to the royal commission. It includes 200 insurance companies, food trusts and corporations like the ABC Packers and the British Columbia Packers Limited. I humbly submit that only a few big speculators can suffer from the intensive development of cooperation. For that reason, any legislation which interferes with the expansion of cooperatives is objectionable.
My final remarks to the house bear upon the problem raised by dominion-provincial relations. On that score we are radical autonomists and we believe that any attempt by any federal government to reduce the prerogatives of provincial legislatures is a step towards the eventual disintegration of the federal compact. Our country cannot reasonably hope to become a unitary state. Two fundamental reasons will always prevent this, namely, the diversity of its population, and the vast expanse of its territory.
	#
Since 1760 one has found in this country citizens of different racial origins, different philosophical ideals, different religious convictions, that is a state of things which will last for all time. In order that legislation may adapt itself in so far as possible to the needs of these various groups, it must be passed and implemented by provincial authorities.
Moreover, it is extremely presumptuous to claim that this country may be administered from Ottawa since it is more extensive than Europe which numbers some thirty governments and since the United States require 49.
These two reasons, in evidence at the time of confederation, still apply and will hold good for all time. It is our duty, as was so aptly pointed out by the hon. member for Beauce (Mr. Dionne), to let the provinces look after their own obligations and sources of revenue. We have been given to understand that Ottawa seeks to centralize taxation so that it may meet dominion expenditures. This argument does not convince me since, looking over the budget now before the house, I find that out of $2,769 millions, a little over ten per cent, that is less than $300 millions are spent annually on the payment of family allowances, old age pensions and unemployment insurance benefits.
Mr. Speaker, if we wish our people to develop in a friendly and prosperous spirit within the scheme of confederation, we need fulfil only one duty, that is, carry out decentralization. On that condition only will life be tolerable for the various groups settled in this country.

subsubtopic: DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I wish to say something about oil, not the kind that is frequently spread in this chamber, but the kind that comes out of a hole in the ground.
The only direct reference to oil that I find in the budget speech is on page 2919 of Hansard, where the Minister of Finance (Mr. llsley) said:
Other minor amendments to corporation income and excess profits taxes will provide for the extension for another year of the tax credits now granted in respect of exploration expenses incurred in the petroleum, natural gas and mining industries, with an adjustment in the amount of the credit appropriate to the reduced rate of corporation tax and an extension of a tax credit for expenditures incurred in deepening an existing oil well.
I am afraid that the second word of that paragraph, "minor", is only too strongly indicative of the attitude which this government has taken towards oil development and exploration and oil taxation generally.

The Budget-Mr. Harkness
Canada has been described as an oil-hungry nation. We produce only fifteen per cent of our requirements of crude oil, which is less than one per cent of the world's production, and we possess less than one-tenth of one per cent of the world's proven reserves. At the same time we are great users of oil, coming second only, on a per capita basis, to the United States among all the nations of the world. In spite of these facts the present budget does not contain the provisions which have been recommended by the oil men of the country to encourage the exploration and drilling programmes which are required to maintain our present production and discover new oil fields in the dominion.
In order to make the oil situation clear I should like to give a brief review of production in Alberta which is and has been for many years the chief source of oil in Canada.
In 1945 Alberta accounted for approximately ninety-eight per cent of Canadian production, excluding the northwest territories. In Alberta Turner valley has contributed 97-6 per cent of all the oil produced in the province from the start of the industry up to the end of 1945. In passing I may say that I exclude the figures for the northwest territories, where they produced 351,000 barrels last year and about 1,250,000 the year before, because that production was really a defence matter. The oil produced in the Northwest Territories can only be used locally, but of course it is very valuable there, close to where it is found.

subsubtopic: DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Does the hon. member mean at Norman Wells?

subsubtopic: DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Yes. In Turner valley, gas seepages had been observed for many years before the first oil well was drilled. There are stories of cowboys and cattlemen in the early days who, when their business took them into that part of the countiy, would poke a stick into the steep side of Sheep creek and light a match to the gas which came out and cook their bacon and beans over the resulting gas fire. It may be a matter of interest that only last year I saw a small fire of this nature burning on a hillside a few miles north of the Turner valley townsite. It was these gas seepages which indicated the presence of oil and led to the discovery of the first Turner valley well, Dingman No. 1, which was drilled not far from the site of one of these gas seepages. This well struck oil in a shallow horizon above the limestone, in 1914, and started the first Calgary oil boom, during which, for a short period, every place of business in Calgary, practically, was an oil office, and fly-bynight stock promoters were collecting money
in wastepaper baskets. This wave of get-rich-quick stock selling was rapidly ended by the first world war of 1914-18, and oil development languished for ten years, until the famous Royalite 4 well was brought into production with a tremendous flow of wet gas from the limestone. This started a second oil boom and, what is much more important, a great deal of exploration work and drilling, which resulted in a steadily increasing production. This development work was given tremendous impetus when the Home well, some four miles south of Royalite 4, in 1929 turned out a large producer and thus extended the field away to the south. The next few years were ones of steadily increasing drilling and production, with constantly improved drilling equipment and methods, which enabled deeper holes to be sunk. In 1936 Turner valley royalties well, some four miles south of the Home well, struck crude oil in the limestone, and the final period of development of the Turner valley field, as a crude producer in quantity, started. Three years later, crude oil was found in the far north end of the field, so that now production has been secured in an area over twenty-five miles in length.
During the thirty years during which oil has been produced in Alberta, approximately 81,000,000 barrels have been recovered from Turner valley, and approximately 2,000,000 barrels from the rest of the province. During this period, there have been drilled some 654 miles of well in the Turner valley, and something in the neighbourhood of 484 miles of well in the rest of Alberta. I give those figures in miles, because in that way is more readily realized, I think, the tremendous, amount of drilling that went on, than if they were given in millions of feet. This has involved the drilling of over 1,200 wells, of which 460 were producers, 560 were dry holes, or dusters, and the remainder were dry gas producers.
I should like the house to note particularly that only 460 of these 1,200-odd wells were producers. In other words, the oil business is a very risky one.
I think we may now properly ask, how was all this drilling financed? Who was responsible for it? Why was it done? The answer is very simple. Initial production and most of the extension of Turner valley and the discovery of other fields were due to small companies, financed by small men in the financial sense, who were willing to take great risks with their capital in the hope of making large returns. After Turner valley had been proved as one of the great North American oil fields, large companies came into the field, and are now engaged in an extensive geological and geo-
The Budget-Mr. Harkness

physical survey of the foothills area of Alberta, as well as the plains of that province and of Saskatchewan, and as a matter of fact in other parts of the dominion-the maritimes and Ontario. However, the start and much of the important development of the oil business in Alberta were due to the "wild-catter,"as he is generally called. It may also be proper to look briefly at the returns received by individuals and companies responsible for Alberta oil development. The amount of capital risked has been in excess of $150,000,000 and the returns less than $130,000,000, so that the major part of Canadian oil production has been secured at a loss of over $20,000,000 to the enterprisers responsible for it. Furthermore, as nearly as I can determine from examining the figures, all this loss, and more, is due to government taxation in one form or another.
Just at this point I might mention something about the contention of my hon. friends on the immediate left, the C.C.F. party, who in Alberta have been advocating the taking over of these oil wells, and as a matter of fact the whole business of oil development, by a government. I should like to point out that if that had been done the government of Alberta, the dominion government, or whoever had done it would now be many millions of dollars behind, because, in addition to the taxes they have collected1 which, had they been operating the industry themselves, they would not have secured, they would have had this further loss.

subsubtopic: DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: It was just for campaign purposes.

subsubtopic: DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
As the hon. member says, it was just campaign literature.
Furthermore, in connection with the development of oil by a government or a government agency, I should like to mention briefly a -little crown company called Wartime Oils, which the dominion government set up to drill wells in Turner valley, at a considerable loss to the dominion in spite of the fact that they were operating in a proven field.
The point I am getting at there, once more, is that the oil business is an exceedingly risky one, and I think we are extremely fortunate that we have men in Canada who will take the risks involved in putting up the capital required to discover what has been discovered. In view of the loss which has been incurred in searching for oil in this country, is it any wonder that the oil men are discouraged and that a full-out drilling programme is not in progress?

To show it is not, may I illustrate from the situation in Turner valley?	When this
session of parliament began there were thirty-two large rotary drilling rigs in the valley which had been used to drill wells there or other exploratory wells in the foothills. All these rigs were capable of sinking wells to the depth of 10,000 feet or more required in that area. Of these thirty-two drilling rigs only four are in operation and drilling; the remainder are sitting idle. Each of these rigs represents an investment of $150,000 to $200,000, or the twenty-eight sitting idle means between four and five million dollars of idle capital, all of which should have been at work twenty-four hours a day drilling wells and attempting to increase Canadian production. In addition, of course, there is a considerable amount of employment which we might have had and is being lost. Everyone of these rigs would be working if the tax structure were such as to encourage the oil men to drill; but as matters stand at present, only the large companies, whose revenues come largely from refining, and selling and distributing the products, and who own a number of wells now in production, can afford to operate. This is so because present tax credits and depletion allowances cannot be used by the smaller producing companies, or by prospective new ones, to anything like the extent or advantage that they are used by the large companies.
To- illustrate what I mean, assuming that the present budget resolutions pass, let us take a company which secures an income of $1 million from producing wells in 1947. It has a depletion allowance of 33% per cent, which leaves a taxable income of roughly $667,000. The thirty per cent corporation tax on this bill will give a tax bill of roughly $190,000. This company during the year drill one deep test well in the foothills area at a cost of $400,000, which is the normal cost, and if this proves to be a dry hole they get no returns. They are allowed fifty per cent of the cost of this well under the deep test drawback regulations, which of course would be $200,000-$10,000 more than their tax bill-and as a result, the company would pay no taxes. Further, of course, it means that the cost of this dry hole to the company was only $210,000.
Let us take a new company which is formed and which drills a similar well costing $400,000, which proves to be a dry hole.- The cost is $400,000. They have no way of getting out of it. Similarly, a small company with an income of $100,000 a year from producing wells would have done the same drilling at a cost of S381.000. From that

The Budget-Mr. Harkness
example we see clearly that the present tax provisions work out to the advantage of the big company but do not he4p the little fellow.
The plain truth of the matter, put as simply as I can state it, is that no encouragement is given to new capital to go into oil drilling enterprise, and the tax provisions are such that small companies with a limited income from production, or none, and with a fair amount of cash, are not in a favourable situation. There are many companies of that kind, which have no producing wells or only a very small income from producing wells, but from their production in the past they have a fair amount of cash. They are not justified, however, in risking that capital in an attempt to get new production at the present time. As a result they sit there and the drilling equipment is idle. They are doing nothing. Of course the ultimate position is that only a fraction of the drilling that could be carried out is going on in Alberta.
I should like now to make some suggestions to the minister as to how the oil business could be stimulated by government action. These suggestions are essentially those of the Alberta Petroleum Association, which includes in its membership practically all the independent oil producers of Alberta as well as the large companies. When we refer to the independents in Alberta we mean the small companies apart from Imperial, Standard, Shell and so on.
The first of these suggestions is the matter of deep test legislation. A tax deduction of fifty per cent is allowed for expenditures made in drilling deep test oil wells. This deduction is allowed only for wells in the foothills area which involve drilling to a depth ranging from 6,500 to 12,000 feet or more. These are the depths necessary. The oil men would like to see this interpretation of the tax provision changed to include the deepening of abandoned exploratory wells. The question I should like to ask the minister is whether the statement he made does or does not mean that. I am not clear on the point and I should like to have him answer that.
In any event, a considerable number of these abandoned wells did not reach the oil producing limestone, for one reason or another, and their inclusion in the tax deduction provisions would result in some of them being completed, any one of which might,
if successful, give us another Turner valley. The oil men are anxious that the fifty per cent tax. deduction be extended to wells drilled in the plains area, most of which do not go deeper than 3,500 feet and, for the most part, less.
The adoption of this suggestion by the government would do much to encourage drilling in the Alberta and Saskatchewan plains area. Why such wells do not enjoy this tax benefit I cannot understand, because an oil well at 2,000 feet is as valuable as one at 9,000 feet. I suggest that the government should do everything possible to get a large drilling programme under way on the plains where production has already been undertaken.
In 1945, in the plains fields of Alberta there were produced 630,000 barrels of oil, which went a considerable way toward offsetting the decline of nearly 900,000 barrels in Turner valley in 1945 as compared with 1944. At this point I would point out that Turner valley has passed the peak of production. That occured in 1942, and since that year it has been steadily and rather rapidly declining as an oil producer. It is for this reason particularly that it is so essential to open up new fields.
At the same time I wish to make it clear that the valley will produce a large volume of oil for many years to come under a favourable tax structure, and many more wells could be drilled there which would prolong the life of the field. As a producer, Turner valley compares favourably with the major United States fields, and as a result of its performance Canada since 1939 has taken second place in the British empire as an oil producer, and has also taken its place among the oil producing countries of the world.
Let me get back to my suggestions. The first is that the extension of the fifty per cent tax deduction to wells drilled on the plains and to completing abandoned wells will at once materially increase the number of wells drilled.
Secondly, there should be a greater depletion allowance. At the present time operators are allowed a depletion allowance of 33jr per cent. In the United States they are allowed up to fifty per cent and in no case less than a depletion allowance determined by the rate of production to available reserves in relation to the time of investment. This means that a company having no net income in any particular year is entitled to a depletion allowance and may carry it forward or backward to apply against future or past profits.
The Budget-Mr. Harkness

Some of our mines were at one time allowed a depletion allowance of fifty per cent and I understand that they are pressing strongly to have that restored. I would press strongly that the provision be put in for oil drilling whether it applies to mines or not. Mining is surely not as hazardous or as risky as drilling for oil. A mine is usually developed only after a large body of ore has been found, but the only way that oil is found is by the drill and there is always the possibility of a dry hole.
As an example of what the oil men face, even in a proven field, I would read a short paragraph from an issue of the Calgary Herald which I received yesterday or the day before:
Foothills No. 24, recorded a pleasant surprise for oil men when it came in on what was considered the eastern limi t of the north valley field as one of the valley's best, and at latest reports was doing nearly 800 barrels daily under unrestricted flow.
Foothills No. 25 will be drilled immediately a quarter of a mile northeast. Drilling these wells is like walking a plank blindfolded. You never know when you will step over the edge. With the east extension wells you never know when you will have overstepped the fault block. You are dealing with the dark underground mystery of the Turner valley limestone. You are gambling a quarter of a million dollars that it extends one step more. You will have to go over the edge before you can afford to stop drilling.
There have been drilled in Turner valley, since it was proven as a major field, plenty of wells that did not come into production, or that did not realize production which amounted to anything. Then, even when the well is a producer, no one knows how long it will continue, or at what volume. Under the circumstances, I should think the oil drillers ought to be given greater depletion allowances than they have been allowed in the past, and in any event they should get as good a deal as United States operators get in their maximum of fifty per cent.
The third point is that all drilling costs, permit and leasing expense, geological and geophysical costs, etc., be allowed as deductions for tax purposes and, further, that these expenses may be claimed as and when desired, so that large expenditures over two or three years may be deductible when production is secured, and.spread over that production.
The fourth point is that present income tax regulations covering exploration and1 development, which when the present budget is passed will expire on December 31, 1947, should be made part of the permanent tax structure so that operators may be able to make future financial plans under definitely known tax conditions. In the past the existing write-off regulations, depletion allowances, etc., have been subject to renewal, or not, from year to

year. This has made for uncertainty as to what the position might be in future, and has discouraged the small operator particularly.
The fifth point concerns the removal of the subsidies now being paid on crude oil imported into the prairie provinces. The Alberta Petroleum Association contends that to a large extent these subsidies were passed on to the railway companies, and that they have resulted in an artificial depreciation of crude oil prices. They believe that the subsidies should be removed and that Canadian crude oil should be allowed to reach its true economic level. Further, they contend that this will not result in any price increase to the consumer if at the same time the government removes the wartime tax of three cents a gallon on gasoline. In fact, some of the Calgary oil men insist that the price, in Alberta at least, can and would come down if free competitive prices were allowed. To support this, they point to the decrease in the price of gasoline in that province as Turner valley developed and small companies got into the refining business. The great example is the price of gasoline in the Coutts area in the southern part of the province. That price came down materially during the period of Turner valley's growth and development and as small refiners got into operation. About the time the war began the price of gasoline was around twenty cents a gallon. At the present time, owing to various restrictions that have been put on the oil business and the levelling of prices, gasoline now costs thirty-eight or thirty-nine cents a gallon in this area. Of course to a large extent that was due to the fact that one of the large oil companies bought a small refinery which had been established at Coutts and closed it up, and now gasoline has to be shipped into that area. The oil men further maintain-and I think they are right-that under conditions of free competition many small refineries would start up, and as a result the price of gasoline would be brought down.
In that connection they put up the argument, which I think is sound, asking why the government should control the price of gasoline in order to keep it approximately the same throughout the prairie provinces, Alberta, Saskatchewan and Manitoba. They maintain that Alberta should be able to take advantage of its geographical position and the fact that oil is produced there. They say, if that is to continue to be done and Alberta farmers are to be penalized to whatever extent they are penalized, then the government should also take over entire control of the price of wheat, and see that sufficient subsidy is paid so that the same price can be offered for wheat at

The Budget-Mr. Harkness
Didsbury or Olds or Lethbridge that is paid in the Red River valley. There is a considerable differential at present, owing to freight costs, and if that is to be allowed to continue, then gasoline should be treated in the same way.
The government seems determined to keep all information about the subsidies paid very secret, and as a result I am not in a position to say definitely or even to form a good, sound opinion, in regard to the effect on prices of the removal of the subsidy. I have been mentioning the contentions of the oil men; and I think they are right when they say it has been impossible to get from this government information on which a sound judgment could be formed. I placed on the order paper a question which was passed as an order for return on April 17. The information I was given amounted to exactly nothing.
I need not bother reading all the questions I asked; they were in connection with the source of supply of oil imported into the prairie provinces, the amounts from each source, the delivery point, the subsidy paid, the cost per barrel and so on. The reply came back from the Department of Mines and Resources: "No information"; from the Department of Reconstruction and Supply: "No information"; from the Department of Trade and Commerce: " No information." From the Department of Transport comes this information:
The board of transport commissioners advise no information can be given with respect to part 7 of this question because the shipping and destination points are not given.
Of course that is the information that was asked for. Finally, we come to the wartime prices and trade board, and here is what they say:
Subsidy is payable by Commodity Prices Stabilization Corporation Limited where necessary on imports of crude oil from the United States to the prairie provinces in an amount sufficient to reduce the laid down cost to refiners to a level equivalent to the laid down cost of crude oil of comparable grade produced in the Turney Valley oilfields.
What actually happened was that the Turner Valley oil field price was set at a very low level. Subsequently it has been raised forty-five cents a barrel, and the price was just kept at that level. The present price is, I think, $2.08 or $2.11 a barrel, which is an increase of forty-five cents over the price some eight or ten months ago. Then they go on:
In accordance with government policy as stated from time to time in the House of Commons by the Minister of Finance, it is not considered to be in the public interest to give
information as to subsidies paid by Commodity Prices Stabilization Corporation Limited to individual concerns.
The rest of it contains no information at all. Mr. ILSLEY: Is the total subsidy given?

subsubtopic: DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Absolutely nothing is given. I have read everything in this return and, as I say, it amounts to nothing. I might iust as well not have it; it did not give me anything. Why the government should be so cagey about this matter; why they should keep it such a secret; why they will not give us the information in regard to really simple questions like this concerning matters about which I think the general public should know, and about which members of parliament especially should know, I do not understand.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subsubtopic: DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: I have stated the total in the house.

subsubtopic: DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Well, here is the return and it gives absolutely no information at all, except the information that they will not give information.
Unless we can, and particularly in this house, get information along the lines I have indicated, how can we reasonably make up our minds in this matter? How can we form sound judgments? So far as I can see, the matter is on a par with the sort of thing we find concerning many other questions which have been asked, and about which members have been complaining. I am convinced that much of this information is denied in various governmental departments because of regulations and red tape which have been laid down, and which no one seems to have sufficient initiative to get rid of or to break. I should think that in many instances ministers do not want to deny the information sought. But three or four years ago, during the progress of the war, rules were laid down, and they have remained in force. A clerk who is asked for information will say, "Well, there is rule 464; no. we cannot say anything about that. No information is available." The time is long past due when departments should be cleaned out in this regard, and new regulations put into effect so that members of the House of Commons can get the information to which they are entitled.
In any event, so far as the oil subsidy situation is concerned, I am sure of one thing, and that is that the removal of the subsidy and the removal of the fixed price on Alberta crude would cause it to rise in price, and thus stimulate development in the oil business.
In closing, I earnestly request the minister carefully to review the whole oil situation, and to make those changes in the tax structure which will enable this industry to start
The Budget-Mr. Hlynka

on a full-out exploration and drilling programme. From the narrow viewpoint of increasing the dominion's tax revenues, alone, this would be good business, because the increased production which would result would materially increase the amount which the dominion government could and would collect in taxes. From the broad viewpoint of increasing our wealth, removing us from the position of almost complete dependence upon foreign countries for our oil supplies, and reducing our unfavourable trade balance with the United States, the benefits would be tremendous.

subsubtopic: DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, on this occasion I propose to discuss the income tax as it affects farmers, and also to discuss briefly Canada's marketing policy and bread rationing in the United Kingdom.
In the presentation of the brief made to the federal government last March by the Canadian federation of agriculture it is stated at the outset that the federation recognizes that with the end of hostilities the problem of food supplies must move into first place on the world scene. They state:
In fact, never before has the burden of responsibility rested so heavily upon victorious peoples of solving the problem of feeding humanity. Even if human considerations were not uppermost m our minds, there is the stern fact that^ millions of hungry, undernourished and starving people constitute an almost insurmountable barrier to progress.
Then it goes on to say:
Canadian farmers would gladly respond to this urgent call for maximum food production, but without a more adequate labour supply and an immediate improvement in economic returns, they will find it quite impossible to produce to capacity.
That is the statement which appeared in the brief presented to the government last March by the Canadian federation of agriculture.
In addition to that, we have the statement made in the house on June 17 by the Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King) upon his return from the United Kingdom. The Prime Minister repeats practically the same story which is told in the presentation of the Canadian federation of agriculture. At page 2530 of Hansard he is reported in these words:
May I add that it does seem to me conditions in central Europe are deteriorating rapidly and greatly . . . Unless some means can be found whereby the new world and countries that have supplies of food and clothing, can furnish those supplies to the people of some of the occupied zones and other parts of Europe, there may be conditions of famine, of strife and of turmoil 
which will amount to something in the nature of the spread of a new revolution throughout Europe.
And farther on, he says:
The last word I should like to say at the moment is that, as far as one can judge what will go farther than anything else in helping to meet present world conditions is increased production and more effective distribution.
He concludes his remarks with this statement :
Anything that can be done in the world to-day to furnish the necessities of life to those parts of Europe which are in dire need will not only mean, salvation for them, but may well be in the nature of salvation for the world as a whole.
After the Minister of Finance (Mr. Ilsley) had brought in his budget on June 27, and after I had an opportunity not only of listening to it but of reading it, I must say I was disappointed lo find that it did not reveal any trace of a recognition of the problem of famine faced by the world to-day.
In the presentation of the Canadian federation of agriculture were eight specific requests respecting taxation. Before setting forth these requests, I should like to read one sentence from the brief, wherein it states:
A number of features of the present act have proved unduly burdensome and in some cases quite unjust to our farmers.
In other words, the federation, an organization which more or less coordinates all farm organizations in Canada, and which represents about thirty per cent of our total population, tells the government that the tax structure of Canada is such that it proves unduly burdensome. Therefore the federation makes eight requests. I shall read them, leaving out the less important parts, so as to have on record what agriculture asked for, and what it received in the present budget. The requests of the Canadian federation of agriculture were as follows:
1.	That the income of the farmer, for income tax purposes be assessed on the basis of an average over a period of at least four years. A moving average plan might be adopted which would assist the taxpayer in meeting payments in years of loss or low returns.
2.	That breeding herds be recognized as a capital asset, and that a basic herd plan be adopted to distinguish between capital and income in live stock dispersal sales.
3.	That the exemption for single persons be raised to $1,000, and that for married persons to $2,000.
4.	That more adequate allowance be made foi the labour of farmers' wives, sons and daughters in connection with production on the farm.
5.	That farmers be no longer required to accept responsibility for collecting income tax from their hired help.
6.	That the government provide a board of arbitration- whereby taxpayers may have a simple and inexpensive means of appealing decisions of income tax officials.

The Budget-Mr. Hlynka
7.	That payment of arrears of interest and principal on the home farm, due before 1940, be allowed as deductions for income tax purposes.
8.	That provision be made for final clearance to be given all taxpayers two years after the final returns have been made for any one year.
One would think that the Minister of Finance would have recognized the contribution made by Canadian farmers during the war; would have recognized and realized that Canadian farmers, particularly those in the west, faced ten years of depression just before the war; would have recognized and realized further that farm machinery just about broke down during the war years, that homes must be repaired and built, that fences must be repaired and built, that house furnishings must be provided, that everything needed in a home on a farm must be paid for at the present time. Yet the minister granted only partly one of the requests which the Canadian federation of agriculture placed before him, that is, the spreading of income tax over a period of three years, not the four-year period as was suggested by the federation. We need food at the present time when half the world is starving and when the British government has been forced to ration bread, but we are not encouraging the production of food by bringing in a budget of this sort and entirely ignoring the farmer. That sort of action discourages food production.
I understand that the Canadian federation of agriculture has been in existence for approximately ten years. I submit that it would be advisable for the government seriously to consider making an annual grant to national farm organizations like the Canadian federation of agriculture. I am quite certain that hon. members will agree with me when I say that Canadian farm organizations have played an important role in the economic life of this country, both during the war and during the peace. Representatives of agricultural organizations have been asked to sit in consultation with the various boards and branches of government, such as selective service. These organizations have been asked to make recommendations and appear as witnesses from time to time in connection with matters of great concern to Canada. These organizations do a considerable amount of valuable research and they print and distribute much valuable information. Hon. members often quote from material and statistics compiled by these organizations and their figures are usually regarded as being authoritative. Various briefs and press announcements dealing with the problems of agriculture are prepared by these organizations. In this way the farm organizations not only are rendering a great service to the farming population of this country, but are rendering a great service to the population of Canada as a whole.
An organization such as the Canadian federation of agriculture has done a great service to Canada by having remained non-political. That in itself constitutes a guarantee that this farm organization will serve a useful purpose in prodding the government in connection with matters affecting our economy regardless of which party is in power. In view of that fact I earnestly plead and recommend to the government that an annual grant be made to this most important farm organization to enable it to carry on research and publish material for the use of our Canadian people. It would be a worth-while investment and would enable our agriculturists to be well informed on matters on which they should be well informed. I make this suggestion and request in all earnestness.
Before I deal with marketing, I should like to say a word or tv%, more in connection with taxation as it affects our farmers. I have received a great many resolutions from organizations in my own constituency of Vegreville. I believe that farm organizations should be encouraged to send resolutions to their members and to the government in order that they may become more keenly interested in the various problems of agriculture. They should be urged to continue and intensify the representations they make to the government and to their representatives in the House of Commons. I should like to place on the record a list of the farm groups in my constituency which have sent resolutions to me fequesting an adjustment in the income tax as it affects farmers. I believe that these resolutions were patterned on the one prepared by the Canadian federation of agriculture and presented to the federal government on March 28, 1946. This is the list:
Pine Knoll Farm Forum
The following Alberta farmers' union locals: Mundare, local 711; Victoria, local 386; Smoky Lake; Brody, local 92; Pakan; Toporetz, local 350; Smoky Lake, local 425; Lampburg, local 101; Chipman, local 75; Andrew, local 8; Mundare, local 145; Woodgrove, local 151; Hillock, local 340; Willingdon, local 1; Lamont, local 192; Sandy Lake, local 27; Errol, local 195.
Mr. Fred Stelter, of Lamont, also sent in a resolution on behalf of a large number of farmers in his district.
These resolutions should not have been ignored by the gentlemen who were drafting the budget. Most of these eight requests that were placed before the government could have
The Budget-Mr. Hlynka

been granted if the government was really and truly anxious to expand production in this country.
I now come to marketing. Over the past two years both the Minister of Agriculture. (Mr. Gardiner) and the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. MacKinnon) have been vigoriusly defending the government's policy of selling Canadian wheat in the neighbourhood of sixty-three cents lower than the United States farmers received who sold their wheat to the same customers. The Minister of Agriculture pacified our Canadian farmers by promising them, if they continued selling at that lower price, a steady market for their wheat in the future.
What are the facts? A Canadian Press dispatch, which appeared in the Winnipeg Tribune of July 3, 1946, gives the following as the reason for the failure of the British food mission to reach an agreement with the Canadian government:
High government officials told the Canadian Press the suspension (of the negotiations) had resulted from reluctance of the Canadian government to commit itself to large-scale wheat shipments which might in the event of a poor crop year in the future prevent her from fulfilling contracts with other customers for Canadian grain.
That dispatch gives what is generally regarded as the reason for the failure to reach an agreement with the British government. But on looking over another newspaper report which appeared in the Toronto Evening Telegram of June 25 last, I find this statement:
Mr. Straehey agreed that it would only be proper for the British government to recognize what this country has done during the war i* supplying wheat and to make a new contract, but he emphatically stated that it would not be of an exclusive character with the United Kingdom filling its entire requirements from this country.
That statement presents an entirely different picture from the one which the Canadian government gives in the first dispatch I quoted.

subsubtopic: DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: That statement did not come from the Canadian government.

subsubtopic: DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: The dispatch says that' high government officials told this to the Canadian Press.

subsubtopic: DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: That is the usual press way of saying they saw somebody.
