subsubtopic: DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
I take it that the second dispatch by J. H. Pisher appearing in the Toronto Evening Telegram gives the real reason. Yet the Minister of Agriculture and the Minister of Trade and Commerce for
fMr. Hlynka.]
years have been asking our Canadian farmers to sell their wheat below the price which United States farmers were getting on the same market in order that we might be able to hold that market for Canadian wheat. Now, according to the statement of Mr. Straehey, that theory has fallen down; it does not hold good any longer. So why should our Canadian farmer continue to sell his wheat below the price which the United States farmer gets if the former is not guaranteed a future market for his wheat? I feel that Canada can afford to sell her wheat to Britain at the price at which she is selling it to-day or even lower, but not at the expense of the Canadian farmer alone. The whole nation should help to bear the burden by means of a subsidy or whatever you wish to call it, and hot footed by the Canadian farmer alone. The policy of this government may have been responsible for failure to reach an agreement.

subsubtopic: DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: May I ask the hon. gentleman a question? Is he making these statements on the assumption that there is not going to be any contract made with Britain?

subsubtopic: DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: No.

subsubtopic: DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Then why is he assuming that there is failure?

subsubtopic: DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
I was just coming to the point which the Minister has in mind. In the Ottawa Journal of July 16, 1946, just the day before yesterday, there appeared this item:
Indications last night were that the Anglo-Canadian wheat agreement would be signed before the end of the crop year, July 31.
It will be for four years, it wras learned, with a fixed price of $1.55 a bushel, basis No. 1 northern, at the head of the lakes for the first two years and no ceiling price for the second two years, but possibly a floor price.
It appears from that report that an agreement will be reached, but that is not the point I was making. My point was that the theory that has been advanced in this house for years by the government, that if the Canadian farmer sells his wheat at a lower price than the United States farmer he will be guaranteed a market for the future, no longer holds; it has fallen down. For that reason I personally believe that the Canadian farmer should demand a price for his wheat comparable with the price which the United States farmer receives, and if the Canadian government wants to sell our wheat below that price, it is up to the whole country to subsidize that price.

The Budget-Mr. Hlynka

subsubtopic: DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: May I ask one more question? Assuming that the agreement when it is made and signed provides for the selling of all the Canadian wheat which any authority who is competent to judge thinks ought to be sold under such a contract in each year for the period of the agreement, would the hon. member still make the criticism he is now making?

subsubtopic: DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: It depends upon the price.

subsubtopic: DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Even if the price were $1.55 for the first two years and no ceiling on the price for the last two years?

subsubtopic: DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: That does not get the minister out of the hole into which he has got himself by promising the Canadian farmer a guaranteed market for his wheat.

subsubtopic: DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: I have not got myself into a hole. I am simply trying to help my good friend-although we do not always agree politically-out of the hole in which he has got himself.

subsubtopic: DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
I know the Minister of Agriculture is a good friend of mine, but I have many good farmer friends too, and I want to plead their case because I know they are being taken for a ride.
However to leave that for a moment, may I now refer to a press report about bread rationing in Britain. The title is:
Ration bread in Britain on July 21.
If the British government were so certain that an agreement could be reached, and that the British people would be sure to get all the wheat they want from Canada-of course, we may not be able to fill all their requirements-I am not so sure that the British government would have proceeded to ration bread. By the way, I find in the Evening Citizen of to-day an editorial in part as follows:
Housewives Ask the King
When 300,000 United Kingdom housewives petitioned the king last week asking him to abolish the rationing of bread, they exercised a right recognized as long ago as the Magna Charta and constitutionally confirmed by the Bill of Rights of 1689.
It just goes to show that even the housewives of Britain had to petition the king not to ration bread.
I want to quote a passage or two from a press dispatch:
London, June" 27.- (CP)-The government announced to-day that bread rationing in Britain wfill begin July 21.
John Strachey, food minister, told the House of Commons that flour also will be rationed as from that date.
Further down in the article it is stated:
The ration of bread will be nine ounces a day for adults generally, 15 ounces for male manual workers, 11 ounces for expectant mothers and women manual workers, 12 ounces for adolescents from 11 to 18 years, eight ounces for children from 5 to 11 years, four ounces for children from 1 to 5 years, and two ounces for children under one year.
The basic ration is one onuce a day less than had generally been forecast.	[DOT]
Mr. Strachey said the cabinet decided on rationing

first bread rationing in Britain's history . . .
The last statement is this, in reply to Mr. Churchill:
Mr. Strachey: I assure this house and, I hope, the world that the fact that we have faced the necessity of introducing bread rationing is the best proof that we are concealing no stocks of bread or flour or wheat in this country . . .
That places the picture before this house as clearly as I can place it. I maintain, Mr. Speaker, that it is in the interest of Canada to reach an agreement with the United Kingdom on wheat, regardless of the price which Britain can pay; of course she will not take it for nothing. If the United Kingdom buys our wheat the Canadian government should subsidize or make up the difference between the price which the British government will pay and the price which the Canadian farmer should get. Unless we do that, our Canadian farmers will be compelled to continue receiving less than the United States farmer does from the same customer. We all know that the Canadian farmer deserves to get every cent it is possible to get out of the sale of his wheat.
I notice that farmers were urged by the Canadian wheat board to deliver wheat as early as possible. Also the Minister of Trade and commerce (Mr. MacKinnon) rose in this chamber and lauded the attitude of the farmers; according to press clippings, "MacKinnon lauds prairie farmers." The prairie farmers can do pretty well without lauding, but they want a little cash, and I believe we should get on to a basis which would place the farmer in an economic position where he no longer would be forced out of his home by mortgage companies and so forth.
In addition to that, I want to mention the raising of prices on farm machinery. That is in addition to the refusal of this government to grant the farmer these income tax exemptions. I wish also to refer to freight rates. What about the freight rates which western farmers have had to bear for so many years? I believe the time has come when this government should take a bold stand and show that they are really concerned with the future of our agriculture. Then what about the price of gasoline?
The Budget-Mr. Aylesworth

All these things add up to the fact that the farmer is in such a position that sooner or later he will not be able to stand on his own feet, and will have to get into debt again.
I therefore appeal to the Minister of Finance and the Minister of Agriculture tp consider once again during this budget the position of the farmer and see if some amendments cannot be brought in to place our agriculture on a really sound basis.

subsubtopic: DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in rising to take part in this debate I feel that I must speak on behalf of the forgotten man-the farmer. He has been carrying far more than his rightful share of the burden during the war years and is still being asked to carry on and produce more and more, and he is given very little consideration when it comes to price control.
The Minister of Finance (Mr. Ilsley) has said that the thing which would prevent a depression would be greater production. I would say that this government has done nearly everything that could be done to discourage production.
For instance, the ceiling^ price which was put on meat has"~Been wrong from the very start. I asked this government three years ago to raise the ceiling on beef two cents a pound to the farmer and to leave it as it was to the consumer. If that had been done we would not have had the black market experiences we have had. There was too great a spread in price from what the farmer received for his meat and what the consumer paid. When the ceiling price was set I warned the government that this spread of seven cents i pound was at least two cents a pound too much and that when meat got scarce it would cause a black market because, the retailer having a spread of seven cents, it would bring him a return, on a 500-pound carcass of beef, of $35 profit, which was too high when compared with the price the farmer had to take. For example, a 1000-pound steer would bring the farmer around S100. He had to take care of that animal for at least two and a half years-buy feed and provide other incidentals. Compare this with the retailer, who would cut and sell this carcass over the counter in possibly two hours for 835 profit. If the ceiling had been raised two cents per pound it would have given the retailer a profit of $25 instead of $35, and the retailer would not have had the $10 to pay the wholesaler over and above the ceiling in order to get meat to sell in his store. Also, if this had been done the farmer would have received1 $10 each

more for his cattle and the consumer would have had his meat for the same price as he has been paying. Instead of this, we have had for the past year the greatest black market this country has ever seen. It has become a joke.
This government has set up many boards of control, and the result is that the farmer has to have a permit for nearly everything he wants to do in connection with the operation of his farm. First, he is forced to obtain a permit to kill, even if he wishes to kill his own stock; then, he is, if lucky, given a quota of the number of carcasses a month he is allowed to handle, which in the case of hogs runs from two to ten a month, and yet some permit holders have bragged that they have killed over two hundred' a month. What is the board of control for? Thus the man who tries to live up to the regulations finds himself handicapped as compared with the man who carries on with little or no regard for government regulations, orders or control boards. This situation has caused more dissatisfaction and unrest among farmers than anything else. We are told by the boards that these restrictions have been put on so that we shall use less meat here and be able to send more meat to England. I am going to say that more meat is being used for our domestic market to-day than ever before; much of the meat is being sold at from three to twelve cents a pound above the ceiling, and yet the farmer is asked to sell at the ceiling price.
There is then the question of milk. A few weeks ago the farmers of Ontario asked the government for a raise in the price of milk. What did they get? Here we have something that has far more food value than any other commodity for the price. Compare milk with soft drinks, which have practically no food value. A quart, or forty ounces of milk sells to the public for twelve cents; forty ounces of soft drink sells to the public for twenty-eight cents. I am sure that the government is holding the price of milk far too low, or is allowing the other to sell far too high. I would ask the government to allow the price of milk to be fixed so as to ensure the farmer a fair profit on his investment and a fair return for his labour. In this regard as with respect to the ceiling on meat, it has worked to the disadvantage of the farmer.
Another class of people who need some consideration are the vegetable 'growers. They work long and hard to supply the consumer, but in many instances before they have had an opportunity of disposing of their vegetables, imported vegetables will appear on the market

The Budget-Mr. Aylesworth
and their surplus remains unsold. I would ask the government to give this matter serious consideration and restrict the importation for longer periods each year.
I feel also that the policy of collecting income tax has worked to the disadvantage of the farmer. He makes out his returns and takes or sends them to an income tax office. He is called in and told that his feed bill is wrong, that if he fed that amount he is wasting it>-this from some man who would not know a hog if he saw one, or scarcely knows that his morning bacon is part of a hog, let alone how to feed them. Not many farmers will buy feed to throw it away. In some other cases he has been charged with $125 for each member of his family for food used from the farm. I understand that this has been stopped. I know of some farmers who have been large producers who have gone home from the income tax office where they were called in connection with their return, and have sold most or all of their stock. Why? Simply because they have not enough left to make it worth while. This has adversely affected hog production and it will be felt in the dairy industry also. This is certainly not a time to do anything to cause a decrease in production; it is a time when everyone should be encouraged to produce more than ever before to help save the thousands in Europe from starvation and at the same time help to stave off a depression here in Canada. Production could be increased, for instance, by increasing the price of milk to the farmer. Milk should bring more than it did in the month of May, which was $1.60 per cwt. for 3-3 milk and is below the cost of production. I know some will say that this price is higher than in the past. That is true, but it costs more to produce milk now than it did before the war. Wages are to-day almost double what they were in pre-war days; feed is higher in price; farm machinery has been increased in price; steel has increased in price. In fact, almost everything the farmer has to buy for use on his farm is higher in price. Therefore it is unfair to ask the farmer to produce to-day at present prices. It cannot and, may I say, will not be done.
Labour and the farmer will rally to the request of the government for greater production, if given a fair chance. The farmer did it in the war years and he will do it to-day, if given fair treatment.
If this country wants more butter, the government should raise the price; more cheese, raise the price; more pork and beef, take off the ceiling price and let the market find its level, Take off the ceilings on all farm produce and do away with control boards. I know that all members of this house will
agree that the production of food is the most serious problem facing this country and the world to-day. During the war years the Canadian farmer produced more food than had ever been produced in the history of the country, despite the short-sighted policy of the government, which had him fighting against labour shortages, price controls that were not in line with cost of production and many other controls. All Canada praised his efforts, but he cannot live on praise alone. There must be some action, some planning and some assistance to make the production of food a prosperous undertaking.
I contend that the prosperity of Canada depends upon the prosperity of the farmer. Why? Because the farmer is the greatest market in Canada for all the goods industry can produce. There are more than 700,000 farm homes in Canada, each one in need of the essentials of life and, in addition, in need of so many of the modern conveniences that have become a part of rural life, as well as of life in the cities and towns. We must convince the people of Canada who do not live on farms of this vital fact.
I believe that this budget should have raised the income exemption for married and single people. As presented by the Minister of Finance, it is a disappointment to nearly everyone. It is a fact that we have been carrying on in a piecemeal fashion for the first six months of this year, and no change for the next six months, a promise of some change for 1947-what a budget! The exemptions for married people should have been raised to at least $2,000 and for single persons to $1,000. If this had been done it would have helped the farmer and all others in the lower income brackets. I believe, too, that some allowance should be made for the farmer's wife who helps on the farm, because on many farms the wife takes the place of a hired man and the farmer is therefore entitled to an allowance on his income tax return.
The farmer is also entitled to a fair return on his investment, and once the people of Canada who live in towns and cities are alive to this fact they cannot but fall in line with the policy of putting agriculture in a healthy condition in order to improve their own living. Once a real standard of living is reached for the Canadian farmer, the standard of living as a whole will be on a much higher level. Then the worker will be busy making goods for the farmer; the farmer will be busy producing foodstuffs for the worker, and with people in full employment and earning good wages prosperity will accrue to all.
Suppose someone had said in 1939 that in the next few years Canada would produce
The Budget-Mr. Aylesworth

subsubtopic: DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
(Translation): Mr. Speaker, before this debate is brought to a close, I wish briefly to acquaint the house with the reaction of my constituents to the budget, speech delivered by the Right Hon. the Minister of Finance (Mr. Usley.) The people expected, and reasonably so, a general tax reduction. After having done more than their share during the difficult years of the war to help the government in bringing to victory the struggle undertaken, our workers were desirous of having enough money left out of their pay cheques to enable them to cope with the ever increasing cost of living. In my opinion, the tax exemptions in the case of married persons should have been brought up to $2,500 and in the case of single persons to. at least $1,000; I believe the government should forthwith consider this matter. The working classes are over-taxed and they certainly deserve a little more consideration from the government.
Insofar as the proposed tax on cooperatives is concerned, I must say that the cooperatives of my district have been organized by farsighted and honest farmers who combine their resources in order to obtain a higher price for their products; other cooperatives have been organized by various groups of small wage earners, who combine their moral and financial resources in order to secure necessities of life at a lower price. We should have more than sympathy for such organizations. In my opinion, they should be tax-free because they are only the representatives of the members to whom the directors must report and, after a strict auditing, refund any overpayments in proportion to each member's patronage.
The agricultural cooperative is, in our
province, the necessary adjunct of the farm

The Budget

Mr. Burton
and serves those classes of society that need protection and help to survive. We cannot compare them with those monopolies and trusts that are cooperatives in name only. I therefore protest against that tax, which will not even bring enough yearly income to pay the interest on the billion dollar gifts made to foreign countries. The tax on soft drinks which, after all, is merely a nuisance tax, is another of the levies that directly affect the people, and which should be abolished as soon as possible. There are so many other sources of revenue to which the treasury could resort that we find it hard to understand the attitude taken by the government on the matter.
In concluding those brief remarks, I wish to say a few words about the flag question. It is my privilege to represent in this house a constituency which numbers among the most populous and the most advanced, from the industrial, ideological, cultural and social standpoints, in the province of Quebec. Important towns, perfectly developed, lie close to unmatched rural centres. The representations made by my electors, as well as the reports, resolutions, letters and telegrams I have received from individuals or public bodies lead me to believe that 98 per cent of the 80,000'people in the Chicoutimi district desire and want an absolutely distinctive flag. That is all to their credit.
No union jack, no fleur-de-lis, no camouflage, no old imperial fabric mended with maple leaves, but a new and distinctive flag, symbolizing a sovereign, free and independent nation. A flag we shall be proud to unfurl, which will appeal to our hearts and minds alike, which will be attuned to every patriotic aspiration of a country that has lived, that has suffered and that endeavours to free itself from all foreign servitude so as to give its own ambitions a broader scope, an ever nobler and loftier ideal.
You wish for national unity, you hope that all sections of our population may live in brotherly understanding and work in unison, under a common allegiance, to ensure our national future, well then, give us first a flag which every race represented in Canada may accept, as an emblem of strength, fame and achievement in keeping with the sentiments and wishes of the various ethnical groups making up our population.
A distinctive flag, essentially Canadian, will be a rallying emblem for all Canadians. A hybrid flag, were it named the Red Ensign, would be a symbol of disunity and misunderstanding. We do not want it.

subsubtopic: DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, some lion, members may be anxious to have this debate closed, blit I make no 63260-226
apology for taking the time of the house to voice, on behalf of the people I have the honour to represent, their objections to the budget as brought down by the Minister of Finance (Mr. Ilsley) on June 27.
From all reports I have received thus far, this budget is the most unpopular ever presented to the Canadian people. On the night the minister made his speech I venture to say there were tens of thousands of people, from the Atlantic to the Pacific, sitting by their radios waiting to hear what tribute they would have to render unto Caesar; or rather, I should say, to know how much less Caesar would extract from them. But what a disappointment! Seldom if ever did so many people in Canada expect so much from one man and get so little.
Before dealing with certain features of the budget, I should like to make a few observations. There are times when I find myself in the awkward position of having to defend the Minister of Finance from his own friends and party supporters out in the country. In the past I could do this conscientiously, because if-and I emphasize the word "if"-I were a believer in the capitalist system of so-called free enterprise, I would not know where to go to find a better Minister of Finance. Even the Tory members of the Progressive Conservative party seem to realize that. No doubt they have found it difficult not to receive this orthodox budget with open arms. Would they have done better if the hon. member for Muskoka-Ontario (Mr. Macdonnell) had presented the budget? They might have put a different coloured coating on this bitter pill, but underneath it would have still been the same capitalistic formula: To those wffio have, more will be added thereto, and to those who have not, even that shall be taken from them.
In the matter of price control, I doubt if they would have done much better than the present administration except that in all probability they would have made more noise about the defrosting process. The Tories seem to have a knack for doing a lot of blasting. It will be remembered that in the early thirties they had the one and only R. B. Bennett who was going to blast his way into the markets of the world, but his powder got wet. They now want to blow the lid off the price ceilings; but, afteT listening to their financial critic reply to the Minister of Finance, I could not avoid thinking of the noise made by a harmless fuse on a first of July firecracker that failed to go off.
I should like to deal with the budget as it concerns the taxation oif cooperatives. I want in the most emphatic way possible to

35S4
The Budget-Mr. Burton

protest against the-I was going to say retroactive feature but I know the minister has taken exception, on. a number of occasions during this debate, to the use of that phrase. However, I would remind him that back out in the country the members of cooperative organizations, the farmers who have their little cooperative trading associations, look upon it as a retroactive feature regardless of what the minister calls it.
There is the other factor, the minister's attempt to force all cooperatives into paying a return on the invested capital. I ask: Where is their so-called free enterprise when they are forcing those who find good in the cooperative movement to accept their pagan philosophy that the wages of money must receive the first consideration? That is a vital question in so far as those of us who are in the cooperative movement are concerned. We in the cooperative organizations have endeavoured to build on true cooperative principles, but because of the shortcomings or neglect of the governments of the past there has not been placed upon the statute books of this country a real cooperative act that would give a guide to cooperatives as to what they should do in order to satisfy the government as to what a cooperative really is.
In these cooperative organizations we have one thing which, in my opinion, is the hope and salvation of people in democratic countries. By forming into a cooperative, people are given an opportunity to unite their efforts in self-help. While the Minister of Finance may clamp his finger down on only one section of the cooperative movement, we do not know but that his successor in another year will put the thumbscrews on another section. I should like to give a little illustration of this selfhelp idea, which is to be found in one form or another in all our cooperative organizations.
Back in 1919 there was started north of Humboldt a rural telephone line which I had organized previously. This line was constructed in order to provide telephone facilities to the people in that district. The company was incorporated under the provincial statute as a non-profit-making organization. Over 175 farmers are connected together by the system and we have day and night service for 365 days in the year at a cost of $9 a year. Throughout the years the board of directors have received no remuneration except a per diem allowance for the time spent in attending to the company's business. The shareholders who subscribed for shares have received no dividends, but from time to time money is placed in the reserve account.
It has worked out in this way. We could not wait until the end of the year to collect

from our subscribers the money required to pay the operating costs. We estimated what our expenditures would be, and we made a levy that we considered would be ample with which to pay our linemen, our repair bills and so on. Naturally at the end of the year we had a surplus, but we did not pay any interest on the invested capital, nor did we pay any dividends. If the Minister of Finance wishes I can bring him a file to show that last year this company had considerable correspondence with the department in Ottawa. They had difficulty in getting the department to understand that the company was not a profit-making organization. For a time the department refused to allow them to buy war savings certificates, on the contention that they were a profit-making organization. How do I or any of the members of the other telephone companies in Saskatchewan know that the minister or the Minister of National Revenue (Mr. McCann) will not soon tell us, "You must pay interest on your share capital"?
I should like to quote briefly from a letter I received from a farmer in my constituency, and I can assure the house that this letter voices the opinion of the great majority in my constituency and, I am satisfied, also in the greater part of the west. Here is what he said in regard to the taxation of cooperatives :
The people here are sore about the taxing of cooperatives. They look on it as a raid on the treasury of the cooperatives.
Then again:
Every one knows that the farmers started the wheat pools to save on the costs of marketing, which were excessive. All that the farmer wanted was a fair share of the consumer's dollar and not a profit.
I should like to quote from a letter received, not from a person living in my constituency, but from a man who lives just across the line, in the constituency represented by the hon. member for Rosthern (Mr. Tucker). He is a personal friend whom I have known for many years. He addressed his letter to the Minister of Finance and sent me a copy, thinking no doubt that the minister would be so busy that he would not have time to attend to it. The letter reads:
Hon. J. L. Isley,
Minister of Finance,
Ottawa. Ontario.
Dear Sir:
Re taxation of cooperatives
You are a busy man. In my own way, so am I. I have just read in Hansard that part of your budget speech dealing with the position of cooperatives in respect to income tax. If I read correctly and the House of Commons accepts your recommendation, it is your intention to

The Budget-Mr. Burton
take from me certain moneys that belong to me personally by way of taxing the wheat pools who are holding this money in trust to my account.
I take very strong exception to this action on your part and request that you give me good and sufficient reasons on common sense and moral grounds for your actions.
He goes on:
Let me put my position before you:
(1)	In 1924 I, with my neighbours and other farmers in this province, grouped ourselves together in what was known as the Saskatchewan wheat pool. In that year our grain was handled under agreement with private elevator companies. In many eases this agreement was not lived up to in spirit, if in letter, by many of these companies and proved to be unsatisfactory.
(2)	As a result of dissatisfaction, in 1925 we found it necessary to handle our grain through our own elevators known as Saskatchewan Pool Elevator Company. These elevators were to be operated at cost. Any moneys in excess of actual operation costs were, obviously, a part of the price of my grain and belonged to me personally and at no time were the property of the elevator company.
(3)	In pursuance of this policy of operating at cost, pool elevators in 1925 made no charge for handling and storing of grain at the time of delivery, the policy being to deduct actual operating costs from the final payment to be made when all the grain handled had been sold, plus reasonable reserves.
(4)	My recollection is that on some of the lower grades and mixed grades of grain handled, no final payment was available to make such deductions. The result was that members having such grain got it handled for nothing, which obviously was not fair to other members.
(5)	As a result of this experience, the board of directors quite properly saw the necessity of making a charge for handling and for storing the grain at the time of delivery to the elevators.
(6)	For reasons of safety, and because at the beginning of the grain delivery season it is impossible to accurately anticipate operating costs, handling and storage charges were set at a level greater than was necessary to meet the costs. In other words, part of the proper price of my grain was unavoidably taken from me at the time of delivery.
(7)	This policy of charging an amount for handling of grain at the time of delivery has been followed in subsequent years and has proved satisfactory to me and in line with cooperative principles and sound business practice. The fact that any excess charge greater than operating costs belong to me as the grower of the grain and a proper part of the price of such grain has been accepted by the members through their organization and until just recently admitted and gone unchallenged by your and preceding governments.
He goes on:
Now, I am in complete agreement with you when you say that the profits of cooperatives should be taxed the same as private companies and believe that cooperatives themselves are also in agreement.
May I interject there, so long as we have or may have a cooperative act that will give us all a yardstick to go by, so that we shall not 63260-226J
be subject to the whims of certain individuals or officials, changing from year to year. The letter goes on:
My question to you, Mr. Usley, is, by what process of reasoning do you find that the pools are taxable on moneys that obviously do not belong to them as organizations and which they hold in trust for their members? Obviously, and I think you must agree, such moneys are a proper price of the grain and should become taxable only when they get into the members' hands and they are found to be taxable under the provisions of the income tax laws.
I ask of you a plain and straightforward answer to this question. In closing, may I say that it does seem ingratitude on your part and on the part of your government and a lack of appreciation of the very fair and moderate stand the wheat pools have taken all along in the matter of grain prices at a time when the attitude of privately owned elevator companies must be a cause of considerable embarrassment to yourself and your government.
I wish to say a few words about that flood of postcards which some of us members have been receiving. Here are samples of two different kinds that I received. One of them
says:
I respectfully urge:
1.	That the government apply income taxation on exactly the same basis on all forms of commercial enterprise, including cooperatives, crown companies, municipal and governmental undertakings and mutual concerns.
2.	That patronage dividends, and like payments, be disallowed as an expense before arriving at taxable income.
The other card is of a different colour and is worded a little differently. It says:
Dear Sir:
I respectfully urge that the government apply the same principles of income taxation to all forms of retail business, cooperative and otherwise. I further urge that patronage dividends should not be allowed as an item of expense before computing taxable income.
Yours sincerely
Very appropriately this card bears the name of Mortimer Snerd. That is the way I received it in the mail.
There were, according to the 1941 census, 43,292 people in the constituency of Humboldt. Up to date I have received 253 of these cards. That includes men, women and children, and even those bearing bogus names. Everyone of these cards received by me I acknowledged. A large number of my acknowledgements were returned with the postmaster's notation, "Not called for", or "Unknown here". I diould like to read part of a letter I received from one man in reply to my acknowledgment:
Mr. J. W. Burton, M.P.
House of Commons,
Ottawa, Canada Dear Sir:
This acknowledges receipt of your letter to me dated the 14th instant, in which you acknowledge receipt of a postcard purported to have been signed by me. In reply I would advise

The Budget

Mr. Burton
that I have not signed any of these "request" or "urge" cards that are being. distributed through the mails to the taxpayers of the country. If any such card has reached you under my name it has been signed by someone else than myself.
If the paper shortage is as acute as our government would like to have us believe, why all this tommy-rot and cluttering of the mails in sending out all these cards, many of which may have never been seen by the party whose name is attached to them?
While on the subject of these cards, I want to say that I have always welcomed hearing from the people of my constituency, and I shall continue to look forward to hearing from them. But most of the people in the constituency have known Joe Burton long enough to know they do not need to have some smart aleck in Winnipeg or Toronto prepare their message to me for them. I have lived1 in the constituency for over forty years, and for thirty years I have been an active member of a number of cooperative organizations.
But those 253 cards were not the only communications I received on this taxation question. Over fifty wheat pool locals and other local cooperatives in my constituency expect me to protest vigorously on their behalf against the action of the government in this matter, I shall not weary you, Mr. Speaker, or bon. members by reading all their protests. I shall read only this one as an example, and may I remind the house that the total membership of the local cooperatives I have just mentioned in my constituency is many times greater than the number of cards I received, which were prepared evidently by the so-called income taxpayers association. This letter expresses what they are protesting against generally:
We the members of Quill Lake and Valley Plains Local, strongly protest this move by opponents of the cooperatives, and we wish to bring to the attention of our member of parliament the fact that the farmers of Humboldt constituency are definitely in overwhelming majority in favour of exemption from taxation of patronage dividends in the hands of cooperative organizations, and further, we respectfully request your full support of our views when this matter comes before the house.
May I say, when they ask for exemption from taxation of patronage dividends they do not want to have taxes applied to moneys which are being held for them in trust by their respective cooperative organizations.
I have here a notation that the hon. member for Inverness-Richmond (Mr. McGarry), speaking during this debate, said, as reported in Hansard, at page 3540, in reference to Doctor Coady, who is connected with the cooperative movement in the maritimes:
Doctor Coady has been the organizer, the initiator and the developer of the cooperative

movement throughout the maritimes. He is now and has been for many years the director of that movement.
From what I have heard, Doctor Coady is the director of the extension department of the St. Francis Xavier university at Anti-gonish. It is quite true that he has taken an active part in the organization of cooperatives, but as far as I can find out he is not listed as director of the cooperative movement in Nova Scotia. However, to come to what is more pertinent, the hon. member for Inverness-Richmond said:
What does Doctor Coady say of the legislation dealing with cooperative taxation? He has said it over the radio; he has expressed it in the press. This is what he said: "I am well satisfied with this legislation."
I do not know Doctor Coady personally, but I have heard a lot about his good work; and, having heard and read what the hon. member said in that regard, while I do not doubt his honesty of purpose, I do question the exact attitude of Doctor Coady, if that is the way it was expressed. Why would the cooperative union in New Brunswick, which is part of the movement that Doctor Coady helped build up, have already sent in a protest, as I understand they have done, against this new proposal? Why would the cooperative movement in the province of Nova Scotia, in the organization in which Doctor Coady, again, has been a main driving force, be worried about this and be considering sending in a protest against this legislation? The only explanation which I can think of as to the quotation attributed to Doctor Coady is that probably, on the night the minister delivered his budget speech, some newspaper man got Doctor Coady on long distance telephone or telegraphed and told him that the patronage dividends of cooperatives would not be taxable, without giving him all the other little details; and on hearing that, Doctor Coady possibly said that that would be fine; he was well satisfied. But I doubt if Doctor Coady will be satisfied when he has the full information before him.
One more thing while I am dealing with quotations. On July 10, when the hon. member for Lake Centre (Mr. Diefenbaker) was speaking, he said, after an exchange between him and my leader, the hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar (Mr. Coldwell) and several others:
That, of course, is the length to which my hon. friend, the leader of the C.C.F. party, has gone in this discussion. I can say that he may not be a Conservative, but, as the head of one of the greatest cooperatives in the province, he has indicated the support he would give to my hon. friends of the C.C.F. who have en-

The Budget-Mr. Burton
deavoured to make the cooperative movement in Saskatchewan or elsewhere an annex or an adjunct of the party they represent.
As a member of cooperative organizations in Saskatchewan throughout all these years, I emphatically deny that we of Saskatchewan have in any way endeavoured to bring in the cooperative movement as an auxiliary of the C.C.F. party. I will say this much, that many members of the cooperative movement support us; I as an active worker in cooperative movements have from time to time worked with Liberals and Conservatives, and at no time did any of us attempt to bring politics into our cooperative organization meetings or any of our work. About the best example of cooperation which the hon. member for Lake Centre might experience is when, a year ago last June, some Liberals in the constituency of Lake Centre joined with the Conservatives to elect him, and defeat an outstanding cooperator in the province of Saskatchewan.
Mr. Speaker, on behalf of the people I have the honour to represent I express regret that not more consideration was given to those in the lower income brackets when the minister brought down his budget and announced a new schedule that is to go into effect six months from now. I have always contended, and so have .all members of this group, that the first charge on the production of a nation is a decent standard of living for the people who make that production possible. The Minister of Finance and the Minister of National Revenue (Mr. McCann) know, as well as do all other hon. members, that $750 exemption for a single man and $1,500 for a married couple will not give a decent standard of living. When people earn enough to be able to pay the tax over and above having a decent standard of living the majority, it will be found, will be prepared to do so.
I see my time is going on, and there are a few other things I wish to discuss. I just want to say to you, Mr. Speaker, and all hon. members that some day I am going to take a little time out and tell you two things. One is what we in the C.C.F. mean and would do in so far as social ownership of property is concerned ; and the other is, to give you a straightforward, clear-cut example of what a C.C.F. government in Canada, namely in the province of Saskatchewan, is already doing in that respect. But I shall have to leave that until some other time, because I have a matter here with which I think I should deal. I can assure the house that it is not wholly a pleasure in so far as one part of it is concerned.
Speaking on July 16, the hon. member for Charlevoix-Saguenay (Mr. Dorion) took part in this debate. There is one part of his speech with which I can agree. When he was referring and objecting to the taxation of cooperatives he said this, at page 3519 of Hansard:
I submit that the best way to ensure our population against the dangers of supporting subversive doctrines, is to give them the means and opportunity of acquiring a measure of wealth and becoming landowners.
Since it is difficult if not entirely impossible to conceive of all citizens individually acquiring property, we may. as an alternative, encourage them to joint ownership; such is the function of cooperative societies.
Further on, he said:
The budget, however, ignores this principle; that is why, among several other reasons, I cannot approve the financial scheme as it was brought before us.
I am sorry that the hon. member is not in his place at the moment because, while not agreeing with other parts of his address, I should like to congratulate him on that statement, and other hon. members as well who have spoken in the same vein. I assure them that when they speak like that, whether in the French language, in English or in any other language, that is language that we cooperators can understand. I regret, however, that the hon. gentleman considered it necessary to put on the record a dispatch from Regina as it appeared in Le Droit on July 11 regarding the address made by His Excellency P. J. Monaghan, Archbishop of Regina, wherein he is reported to have accused the provincial government of Saskatchewan of appointing communists to high posts in the department of education. The quotation used by the hon. member can be found in his speech at page 3519 of that day's Hansard.
I regret that I did not have an opportunity to learn French when I was young. That is my loss and no one's gain. However, I could understand enough to know that the quotation which the hon. member was using had1 reference to the provincial government of Saskatchewan, and therefore I made it a point to check on the question he raised. May I say to him-and I hope his deskmate will convey to him what I say in this resipect and ask him to look it up in Hansard-that I have had the privilege of knowing His Excellency Archbishop Monaghan for many years, and I am sure that the archbishop will deplore the fact that the hon. member saw fit to bring this matter into the debate.
May I say again with all deference to the hon. member for Charlevoix-Saguenay that he can rest assured that this question can be
The Budget-Mr. Burton

speakeroldname: Right Hon. J. L. ILSLEY (Minister of Finance):
speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subsubtopic: DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, we have had a long and at times interesting debate on the budget. The criticism has been pretty outspoken, and much of it has been severe. As I have listened to hon. members speaking, I have thought sometimes that they have failed to put themselves in the position of a minister of finance or a government trying to finance a country which has come through five or six years of the most terrible war in human history. Most of the speeches have been directed to the urging of measures which would help here and there, but few of the speeches that have come from the opposition parties in this debate have taken into account the necessity of keeping within our means.
This question was raised by the financial critic of the opposition in the opening speech, when he asked: "Do we or do we not believe in deficit budgeting?" Well, Mr. Speaker, L must say I cannot see how a responsible government or a responsible minister of finance could possibly advocate a system of continued deficits in the Dominion of Canada, that is, deficits year after year, year after year. Therefore the government must in some way, particularly at a time when our national income is as great as it has ever been in the history of Canada, try its best to equate revenue with expenditure. That is the reason we cannot be popular and generous in the fiscal measures we put before the country. If I wanted to popularize myself with the opposition parties in this house I could do so. I could recommend high exemptions; I could recommend large reductions in taxation all along the line; I could budget, instead of for a deficit of $300,000,000, for deficit of a billion or a billion and a half, or something like that. And judging by the tone of the opposition speeches we have heard during the past two weeks, my actions would meet with approval.
I cannot bring myself to do that, even though we have to take a hard course. I know my Social Credit friends think there is another way to do it; that is, by the issue of money. Surely, however, at a time like this even the members of the Social Credit party must realize that this country does not need more money in circulation, or more credit; that this is one of the great contributing causes to the inflationary trend which is so obvious at the present time. So we are
brought back to this, whether we like it or not and whether or not it is popular; we are brought back to the necessity of equating revenue and expenditures when we have high employment and a high national income.
The Conservative opposition has attacked our expenditures. The C.C.F. opposition has shown no concern about our expenditures. Indeed I want to say to the C.C.F. opposition that I do not think in any of their speeches they have faced up to the real problem confronting the government of Canada at the present time. In many respects their speeches are highly intelligent. I do not want to be considered condescending or patroninzing in saying that, because I enjoy listening to them; but they never come down to this: How would they finance? That is the question they never answer. With regard to the Progressive Conservative opposition, they meet this problem by saying that we should cut our expenditures.

Puny stuff, as my hon.
friend says. However, that point has been met during the debate by speeches from this side of the house, and I do not propose to go into it again. There has been some criticism of the fact that these cuts do not take effect until January 1 next, and it has been urged that our new income fax cuts should take effect on July 1, 1946. Well, what were the reasons why we proposed to institute these reductions in taxation on January 1, 1947, instead of July 1, 1946? To begin with, we legislated for 1946 in October of 1945. We made a sixteen per cent cut in our income tax and very heavy cuts in our other taxes in the October budget of last year. The cut for 1946 was provided for then. Some references have been made to promises implied, or something of that kind, by myself that any reductions in this budget would apply to the current calendar year; but no such promises have been read or cited or quoted, nor can any promises to that effect be quoted because I know pretty well what I have said. As I say, 1946 was legislated for by the budget of October 12, 1945; but there are other
The Budget-Mr. Ilsley

reasons. One reason is that had we instituted the reductions in income tax effective July 1, 1946, our deficit, instead of being $300,000,000, would have been very much greater than that; and the responsible critics of the budget in this house do not believe, and I agree with them, in deficit financing. Therefore we had to take into account our financial necessities.
It must be remembered that we changed our income tax system here in 1943. From 1917 to 1943 when income tax changes were made they were effective the current year, because the taxes paid in one year were taxes on the income of the preceding year. That is, in 1935, for example, a taxpayer paid taxes on the income of 1934. But that system was changed in 1943, at a very considerable price. We relinquished 50 per cent of our tax, or something of that kind, in order to get the taxpayers of Canada on the pay-as-you-go, pay-as-you-eam plan. So that now when the taxpayers of Canada pay taxes in a certain calendar year, they are paying on the income of that year, and therefore there is not now the traditional reason for making changes in the income tax system apply to the current year. But there is another very good reason against doing it this year. It is, I think, impossible to put a completely new pattern of taxation into force in the middle of the year. What we have done in the budget of this year is a radical thing, so far as income tax is concerned1. We have immensely simplified it, to begin with. We have raised the exemption. We have dropped the normal tax. We have instituted a different method of fitting family allowances into the taxation system, and we have replaced tax credits with deductions from income when providing for dependents.	[DOT]
When you have a deduction at the source system, and when you have forms in the hands of thousands and tens of thousands of employers in the country who are making deductions from their employee's incomes and you come along with a completely new system in the middle of the year, you create immense confusion. As a matter of fact no government should make a change like that without giving several months' notice.
For that reason it was felt entirely impracticable to institute a new system of taxation during the current calendar year, and that it would be better to have the deductions start in January, 1947. I do not say that you cannot make any changes which affect a current year. You can make a percentage cut. For. instance, you can make a five per cent cut on all taxes, or something of that kind. But I do not think any hon. member
[Mr. Ilsley. 1
would have been in favour of another straight percentage cut. I do not think there would be a member in the house who would be in favour of that. A moderate cut is, I think, all right. We did that. But if you keep that up it is unfair to the low income groups. Therefore we could not attempt another percentage cut. There might be simple changes which you could make during the current year, but not the institution of a new system or introduction of a new pattern of income taxation.
Then there is the question of the provincial agreements. I am not here to put any authoritative interpretation upon these agreements, respecting our obligations to reduce taxation. But I think the relevant clause of the provincial agreements is open to this interpretation, that we must start with the taxes in force on December 31, 1946, and reduce the rate then in force for corporations by ten per cent and reduce the rate in force for individuals by a substantial amount.
If we took $155 million out of our present income tax and substantially reduced our corporation tax in the middle of 1946, we would be in a difficult position if a similar cut were necessary under the provincial agreements at the end of the year. I hope it will be fully understood by the house how important it was and how necessary it was that we should not make the alteration in the middle of the year.
Then there have been criticisms of the reductions in taxation to the effect that they were niggardly. Let us look at that. The reduction for 1947 is very substantial, judged by any responsible standard. In total, including the additional $12 million cost of family allowances it amounts to $155 million, or a quarter of our present income tax revenue. That is the personal income tax. I am under the impression that it is not fully realized that this reduction comes on top of the sixteen per cent reduction that is now in effect and that taken together they represent a total reduction in our personal income tax revenue of $270 million a year, which is over thirty-seven per cent of the revenue from this tax. And mind yot, this is within a year and a half after the end of the war. Furthermore, some 550,000 to 600,000 taxpayers will be removed completely from the tax rolls in 1947, and for those remaining taxable the tax will be back to a level lower than the level of 1941. And when you just look at it you can see that certainly a reduction of that order cannot, with aDy justice, be termed niggardly, particularly when it leaves us in a deficit position.

I have added the average amount of the national defence tax payable in 1941, namely 3^ per cent, to each of the rates in the different brackets. An interesting thing that develops from this table is that in the brackets from zero up to $3,000 of taxable income, the rates in 1947 are greater in all cases than were the rates in 1941. speechtext: I will not ask for time to argue my point, but we are trying to get clear as to the basis of this table. speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subsubtopic: DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
This is not so, because the hon. gentleman applied the national defence tax only to the amount over and above the exemption. He would have to apply it all the way down in dealing with the tax on that $1,000. I cannot spend any more time on that. It has been gone into carefully by the officials of my department and that is the conclusion to which we have come.
I should like to say something about the taxation of cooperatives. Hon. members, particularly hon. members of the C.C.F., have taken a position that is surprising to me, that what we are proposing constitutes an attack on cooperatives. I want to deny most emphatically that the government wishes in any way to discourage the cooperative movement in the Dominion of Canada, or that the government had any intention by this proposed legislation of discouraging the cooperative movement in the Dominion of Canada.
Let me give a recapitulation of the course of events. In 1930 the Income War Tax Act was amended to include the present section 4(p), which apparently was intended to give exemption from taxation to certain types of cooperatives. Over a period of years most cooperatives were exempted from tax under this provision, but the law officers of the crown now advise-they have been so advising for the last few years-that in fact very few, if any, cooperatives are organized or operate on such a basis as to secure this exemption.
In the light of this highly unsatisfactory and unsettled situation, the government decided to appoint a royal commission to bring in recommendations. The members of this commission were selected with some care. The cooperative union of Canada was asked to name a member and put forward Mr. B. N. Arnason, deputy minister for cooperation in the government of Saskatchewan. The Canadian chamber of commerce suggested Mr. J. J. Vaughan, a retired business man. The government itself nominated Doctor G. A. Elliott, professor of economics, university of Alberta, and Mr. J. M. Nadeau of Montreal, who combined both economic and legal training, and as chairman, Mr. Justice Errol McDougall, of the

The Budget-Mr. Ilsley

court of king's bench, Quebec. I think the house will agree that it would have been difficult to select a more representative or more competent commission. We took great pains in the selection of that commission, because we knew the great importance of the work they were undertaking.
This commission heard evidence from one end of Canada to the other. Hundreds of cooperative organizations appeared before it, as did groups opposed to the cooperatives. They heard economists and lawyers; they visited the United States and they visited the United Kingdom. I venture to suggest that never before in Canada has the question of the cooperatives received such a thorough and complete review. After months of study the commission brought in a report which was unanimous on the important points. This was a remarkable achievement. The government would not have been at all surprised if there had been a minority report or reports, particularly from the members of the commssion who had been appointed at the suggestion of the various interests concerned. However, the main recommendations were unanimous, the only qualification being in the form of reservations.

subsubtopic: DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Was the report unanimous? Was there not a minority report?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subsubtopic: DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
No; the recommendations were unanimous. There are reservations, these being by Mr. Arnason, Mr. Nadeau and Mr. Vaughan, which did not affect in any important way the central body of the report. Under these circumstances, the government would be assuming a heavy responsibility if it departed too far from the recommendations of that report. At least that was the view we took and we have followed the report in the main. Of course the government are under no obligation to adopt the report of a royal commission; they may adopt it, they may vary it, or they may reject it. But in view of the fact that this was a good commission and that the main recommendations were unanimous, the government felt that they should go as far as they possibly could in adopting these recommendations, which they did.
The main point at issue always was: Should patronage dividends be taxed or not? As members of this house know, there was an intensive propaganda against the report of the McDougall commission on that question. That was the main question on which this intensive propaganda took place. All these letters, speeches over the radio, postcards and all that kind of thing were on that main and central and important point, as to whether

patronage dividends should be taxed or not. The government has adopted the commission report in that regard. The qualifications are quite small and I shall deal with them.
I can understand people who want to have everything 100 per cent their own way if they can get it, but there must be a little compromise when you have an acute issue of this kind before the people of a country. The commission came to the conclusion that patronage dividends should not be taxed, that they should be regarded as deductions from income. They recognized the fact that there are cooperatives which have no income within the meaning of the Income War Tax Act, that they market the goods of their members on behalf of the members and return everything to the members. In the case of cooperatives which have no income there is no suggestion that there be any tax imposed.
From hearing some of the speeches in the house, one would have thought that we were constructively creating income which was not income otherwise; that where cooperatives are involved we were saying that there must be at least three per cent. The three per cent provision does not apply at all if there is no income of the cooperative; if in fact there is no income, no profits, then there is no taxing at all.

subsubtopic: DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: No profit to the organization, but certainly a return to the member.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subsubtopic: DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
I am talking only about the tax on a corporate body. The only thing we are talking about here is bodies corporate and I am talking about the corporation tax. The commission said that this rule should apply throughout, that any body corporate, cooperative or otherwise, which paid out on the basis of patronage to its members should be entitled to deduct that from its income for taxation purposes. In that way it has the appearance of fairness.
The fact is, of course, that when you make a recommendation of that kind you are making a recommendation which benefits cooperatives but which really does not benefit to any substantia! degree their competitors, private business. The great range of private business in Canada cannot practically pay out part of their profits on the basis of patronage. For that reason the cooperative reaction to the McDougall commission report was pretty favourable. Representations were made that we should not adopt this or adopt that or that we should not adopt it entirely, but it was far more favourable than the private trade reaction to the McDougall commission report, far more favourable than the reaction of the other camp. Even though hon. gentle-

The Budget-Mr. Ilsley
men opposite call us capitalists or say that we are leading a capitalist raid against the cooperatives and make many other wild accusations against the government, having appointed the commission we have adopted its report in its main recommendation, which is that patronage dividends be deducted for taxation purposes.
There was one qualification. That was the qualification of the three per cent. I think I have made it clear that that does not apply at all unless there is true profit in the organization. If there is true profit in the organization we felt that the organization could only have earned that profit by the employment of capital and that it should not. be permitted to pay it out tax-free if by so doing it reduced its taxable revenue below a reasonable return on. the capital employed. We are not proposing to stop any cooperative from paying it out as patronage dividends, or to compel any cooperative to make a return on capital employed. They can pay it out in patronage dividends if they wish; but they can only pay it out tax-free to the extent that it exceeds three per cent on the capital employed. That was the underlying principle in that regard, and I stated it this way in the budget speech:
The principle underlying this rule is that amounts set aside out of taxable income to be distributed in proportion to patronage by a cooperative or company which does not pay at least three per cent on the capital employed in its business contain earnings which arise from the employment of capital and ought not to escape tax entirely. For many cooperatives which pay patronage dividends this modifica-' tion of the commission's recommendation will have little or no effect, for they already recognize an obligation to pay interest or dividends equal to at least three per cent on capital or retain undistributed income on which tax will be payable. Share capital with a limited dividend and with limitation of voting to one share per member rather than one vote per share was a characteristic feature of the plan of organization of the Rochdale Equitable Pioneers Society, the real founders of the cooperative movement. Cooperatives of this character will usually be able to claim the full amount of their cash patronage dividends as a deductible allowance. Any cooperative which does not set aside as taxable reserves or pay as interest or dividends a total amount equal to three per cent of capital employed, will find itself subject to tax on a portion of the amount it had set aside out of its income to distribute on the basis of patronage.
The three per cent may be paid on loans, not necessarily on shares, and if it is paid on loans, then it is a deduction from income for tax purposes if the cooperative has income.

speechtext: If the minister will allow a question,, he spoke of true profit. Would that be only in the case of dealing with nonmembers?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subsubtopic: DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
The commission did not so find, and I cannot so find either. But please do not let us get into a discussion on this now, because there, is a resolution coming before the house on which there can be a full discussion of the three per cent and of certain other qualifications and extensions of the eommissicra's report, such as the three-year exemption for cooperatives, which the. commission did not recommend except as the Minister of National Revenue might direct. I must say that we have tried to be so fair to cooperatives in this matter that I have been a little surprised at the fury of the attack of some members of the C.C.F. on our motives and on our acts in this regard.
One of the recommendations of the royal commission is that to qualify for exemption of patronage dividends all customers must be treated alike. Some exception has been taken to that. Certain members have said that it would be prejudicial to the development of cooperatives. Our feeling is that that danger is very much exaggerated, very much overstated. In fact, we do not feel that there is any substantial danger at all. But I want to say about all this legislation that we must' do something in regard to the taxation treatment of cooperatives. We have had a commission which has been studying the matter for a long, long time, a fair commission, which has attained, a degree of unanimity which is surprising in the circumstances. If this legislation that we are proposing as a result of the recommendations of the royal commission does not work well; if it turns out to be prejudicial to the development of cooperatives, which we do not want it to be, it can be changed. But I would appeal to members of the house not to take a 100 per cent position necessarily on everything, because this is one of the most difficult questions with which any government was ever called upon to deal.	-
With regard to the necessity of patronage dividends being paid on an equal basis to members and non-members, though the government does not consider that the rule requiring equal payment to all customers would retard the development or interfere with the operation of a cooperative, some of the cooperatives seem to have fears of this kind. Therefore the government is prepared to give consideration in committee to whether the rule can be made more flexible without departing materially from the basic recommendations of the commission.

speechtext:
I think that is the most fundamental thing in the whole business, myself.
The Budget-Mr. Ilsley

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subsubtopic: DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
My hon. friend says he thinks that is the most fundamental thing. The whole commission agreed on that unanimously without any reservation or qualification whatever, that members and non-members must be treated alike, and that is the way we prepared the legislation and are placing it before the house. But I have made the statement that I have just made here, and we stand by that statement.
With regard to the past, the taxation of the grain trade, let us have that put straight before the house. I do not know whether all members understand it or not. It has been referred to as retroactive taxation. We are not proposing to introduce legislation which will tax anything which was earned or accumulated in 1944 or 1945 or 1942 or 1943 or any other year. We are not proposing any retroactive tax legislation. The position we found ourselves in, and I think I have explained it to the house, was this. Between 1930 and 1940 or thereabouts, the pools were regarded as not subject to income tax. Shortly after 1940, doubts arose as to whether they were making a profit or not within the meaning of the Income War Tax Act. Their method of doing business had changed between 1930 and 1940, and doubts arose as to whether they were taxable or not. The opinion of the Department of Justice was taken as to whether they were taxable or not, and in 1941 the Department of Justice gave an opinion that one or more of these pools was taxable. It did not touch the question of patronage dividends. In February of 1943 the Department of Justice gave an opinion that patronage dividends could not be deducted from income for taxation purposes. The pools were so advised and1 their competitors, the grain trade, were so advised, because the grain trade had previously received an intimation that they could pay patronage dividends. So that during the years 1944 and 1945 the pools operated in the knowledge that it was the opinion of the Department of Justice that they were taxable on the amount of their patronage dividends. They were assessed, and three or four cases were taken to the courts on that. Now, the statement which I made in the budget was an offer of a compromise of the cases that are in the courts. In fact, to do something about these cases in the courts, we have either to abandon them, or to proceed with them, or to settle them, and we have to act responsibly and with a due sense of our responsibility to the other taxpayers of Canada. Anything else would be indefensible. Whether it would be popular or not, I do not know, but it would be indefensible.

Fortunately, the McDougall commission laid down certain principles which they suggested as a basis for treating cases in the past, back assessments. They laid down what they called the principle of good faith, that if corporate bodies had been led to believe that they were not taxable, that they had not been assessed and so on, and they had ordered their affairs on that assumption, that the income tax administration had given them grounds for that belief, the commission did not think it would be fair to go back and tax them. And we absolutely agreed with that.
But with regard to those that were assessed, different considerations arise. So I made the offer which I did in the budget. Now I want to make it clear to hon. members that this is not part of any proposed legislation, it is not covered by any of the resolutions; it is not something which we are voting on; it is not something that we are passing judgment on at all in this house. This matter of our suggested compromise with the pools is something as to which the government must take responsibility. But as we were dealing with cooperatives, and as it was so important, we felt it was a suitable place to make that offer to the pools, because so far as I know it is only the pools and the grain trade that are affected, that come into this at all.
I want to say just this, that while the language used in the budget may convey the impression that it is "take it or leave it", that is, either proceed with the case or do exactly .as we say, I do not think that would be quite a reasonable position for a government to take. I think, and I have so advised the representatives of the pools, that if they consider there is anything unfair or inequitable about our offer and wish to make representations to that effect we will give consideration to their representation in discussing settlement of those cases. Any settlement, of course, must be on a basis that can be defended to the taxpayers and public of the Dominion of Canada. I am concerned in maintaining integrity in our financial and taxation administration, and that we must do, whatever happens.
I think that is all I have to say on the question of cooperatives. It is an endless subject, and of course in my remarks to-night I can only touch the high spots, I can only cover a few things which have been raised in the debate.

speechtext: And you made a very good job of it, too.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subsubtopic: DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
I wish now to say something about the dominion-provincial conference. It

The Budget-Mr. Ilsley
is one of the most important matters which ever came before the House of Commons, and I want the house to believe me that it took a great deal of work and a great deal of consideration to frame the offer which I placed in the budget speech. The attitude of the government has been described by one or more hon. members as the attitude of a person wielding a big stick. I deny that. I deny that there is any coercion in this offer at all, and I deny that there is any big stick in it.
I want to elaborate that a little. The only justification for an accusation that there is a big stick here would be a state of affairs like this, that we were virtually driving the provinces into this position, that there were undue differences in the aggregate level of personal income, corporation and succession duty taxation as between adhering provinces and nonadhering provinces. I do not know whether I have made that clear or not; but that would be the essence of coercion, that would be the only justification, I should say, for any claim of coercion, that we had so framed the thing that there were undue differences in the taxation burden, that there had necessarily to be undue differences in the tax burden in the adhering provinces and the nonadhering provinces. That is not so. We almost leaned over backwards to see that it was not so, so that this accusation of coercion could not be made.
In the case of personal income tax, a tax credit up to five per cent of the dominion tax is given to taxpayers in a non-adhering province.
In the case of corporation taxes we insist that adhering provinces levy a corporation tax of five per cent.
As for succession duties, while the dominion's succession duties have been doubled, there is a credit of the succession duty paid to the provinces up to one-half of the new succession duties. It would take a long time to explain just the reasons for those three provisions.

subsubtopic: DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Oh, oh.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subsubtopic: DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
My hon. friend is applauding that for some reason or another, but the reason for those provisions is to make sure that there would not be undue or important differences in the aggregate level of personal income, corporation and succession duty taxation in the adhering provinces and the nonadhering provinces. That is the reason for these provisions, and the reason we went that far is so that we could answer the charge that we are wielding a big stick or working
any coercion here. I repudiate entirely the charge of coercion or a big stick. It is entirely unjustified.
